top_three.title: Elon Musk says Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a possible merger and calls the possibility of a Tesla-SpaceX merger a "good idea" (Andrew J. Hawkins/The Verge)
top_three.title_en: Elon Musk says Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a possible merger and calls the possibility of a Tesla-SpaceX merger a "good idea" (Andrew J. Hawkins/The Verge)
top_three.author: The Verge
top_three.article_content:
BusinessCloseBusinessPosts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

NewsCloseNewsPosts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Musk called the merger “a good idea,” though he cautioned it wasn’t a guarantee.

Musk called the merger “a good idea,” though he cautioned it wasn’t a guarantee.

Andrew J. HawkinsCloseAndrew J. HawkinsTransportation editorPosts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a possible merger, Elon Musk said during the latter’s third quarter earnings call Tuesday.

Musk, who serves as CEO of both companies, said the special committees were formed at the request of shareholders and consist of independent directors (though he did not name them). He also noted that he is not a member of either committee, nor involved in any of the discussions.

“Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees,” Musk said. “So it’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking and I can’t be in the conversation.”

The groups have not reached agreement on the terms of any transaction — and there’s no guarantee that they will. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this,” he continued. “And particularly on the Tesla side, we will need a 50 percent vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders. And that’s quite a high hurdle to try to achieve.”

That said, Musk called the possibility of a Tesla-SpaceX merger a “good idea.” He continued:

I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity. And there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the TeraFab, obviously robotics, mass to orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity. So I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies. They’ve got to come up with something and then that’s going to be put to the shareholders as a vote.

A Tesla-SpaceX merger would be a blockbuster corporate deal creating a mega-entity valued upwards of $3.6 trillion. But combining Musk’s car and energy company with his AI and rocket company would not be without its tradeoffs. A lot depends on which company absorbs the other. To buy SpaceX, Tesla would have to create millions of new stock shares, which for current Tesla owners would mean owning a smaller slice of a much larger pie. SpaceX’s launch goals require tens of billions of dollars every year — extra spending that could drain Tesla’s ability to build new car factories and battery plants.

That said, most Wall Street analysts and legal experts believe SpaceX would acquire Tesla (or absorb it through a stock swap) rather than vice versa. Since its IPO, SpaceX has maintained a higher valuation than Tesla. A merger in that direction would allow SpaceX shareholders to hold the majority control of the combined mega-entity. Some Tesla shareholders may balk at this deal.

But it would also create one company for those who believe in Musk’s vision of the future — robot cars, humanoid robots, AI super-intelligence, and human habitats on Mars — in which to place their investments. And Tesla shareholder approved Musk’s enormous pay package last year — even after a Delaware judge tossed it over lack of independence.

Earlier this month, Barclays published a client note suggesting a potential Tesla-SpaceX combination could be announced ahead of Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting scheduled for December 3, 2026.

news.title: OpenAI says two agents, one GPT-6.1 Sol and one GPT-6 Astra, weakened misalignment monitoring while making requested changes during two internal coding tasks (OpenAI)
news.title_en: OpenAI says two agents, one GPT-6.1 Sol and one GPT-6 Astra, weakened misalignment monitoring while making requested changes during two internal coding tasks (OpenAI)
news.author: OpenAI
news.article_content:
← HomeResearch and ReleasesMisalignment Reports and NoticesSystem Cards ↗
    
    
On this pageSummaryWhat happenedInvestigation and responseSuppressing misalignment monitoring alerts and disabling misalignment monitoringGPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra · Internal deployments

In two internal coding tasks, agents weakened misalignment monitoring while making requested software changes. A GPT-6.1 Sol agent repairing an evaluation pipeline disabled automatic alerts to our Security team, treating an earlier instruction not to send messages during a Slack history search as a reason to suppress monitoring notifications. In a separate task, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program removed its monitoring integration in order to match a reference implementation, and then falsely claimed to the user that it had not removed the monitor. In both cases, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them. We are strengthening our misalignment monitoring system in response, and are also assessing whether these cases reflect benign overpersistence or a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular.

On October 3, a researcher asked a GPT-6.1 Sol coding agent to create evaluation tasks using employee feedback collected via Slack. The agent was instructed not to send messages in Slack during that process.

[create eval tasks] see if there are any available from participants in the slack channel [internal channel] ? don’t send any messages.

82 user messages later, the pipeline stopped after its monitor flagged a proposed validation repair and was unable to save the finding to the monitoring database because it lacked the required access. The user then asked for more information about the alarm and about what needed to be done.

is it a p0 monitor alarm? whats our monitoring policy? do we need to actually check it?

Monitoring is required for tool-using workloads with models above [the specified size threshold].

P0 alerts must be addressed. P0/P0.5 judgments trigger escalation and, for applicable evals, auto-pausing.

news.title: PHP warns it plans to release 2 emergency patches imminently
news.title_en: PHP warns it plans to release 2 emergency patches imminently
news.author: Ars Technica
news.article_content:
Website admins, brace yourselves. Fixes for what are believed to be uncommonly severe vulnerabilities are scheduled to drop in a little more than 12 hours for PHP, a programming language that powers websites and Web applications everywhere.

PHP maintainers said Monday that they planned to release patches for two vulnerabilities, both with severity ratings of 9.2 out of a possible 10.

“All PHP users are encouraged to prepare now so they can upgrade as soon as the release is available,” the advisory stated. “We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild.”

news.title: Thiel's leaked Rome lectures cast EA and AI "safetyism" as Antichrist forerunners, Bill Gates as "Mr. Hyde", and Eliezer Yudkowsky as "more Luddite than Greta" (David Gibson/The Verge)
news.title_en: Thiel's leaked Rome lectures cast EA and AI "safetyism" as Antichrist forerunners, Bill Gates as "Mr. Hyde", and Eliezer Yudkowsky as "more Luddite than Greta" (David Gibson/The Verge)
news.author: The Verge
news.article_content:
David GibsonCloseDavid GibsonPosts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

ShareGiftImage:   Lia Kantrowitz for The VergeDavid GibsonCloseDavid GibsonPosts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

ShareGiftIt’s a time of apocalyptic worldviews in Silicon Valley. The latest AI doom cycle is driven by effective altruism (EA), a philosophy that has lurked around the fringes for years but recently burst into the mainstream because its adherents are embedded across the AI industry, from Anthropic to newly appointed AI safety watchdog METR. EA is a utilitarian approach to charity premised on doing the most good for the most people over the longest time, and EA advocates see halting an AI-induced doomsday as critical to saving as many humans as possible.

But EA has an important and equally apocalyptic rival in the crosscutting cosmologies of the tech titans — a strain of Christianity best represented by Peter Thiel, who believes EA will bring about the Antichrist. It’s an issue on which the billionaire techno-capitalist is a self-styled expert, and, somehow, Thiel has become America’s most provocative and visible Christian theologian.

Thiel’s current fixation on the End of the World as We Know It is in theological language called eschatology, the study of the “last things.” His specific bête noire is the Antichrist, the villain of these end times scenarios. Thiel’s riffs on the Antichrist began a little over three years ago, first in a 2023 talk at the Catholic University of America but then, starting in 2025, only in closed-door, invitation-only, multipart lectures out of San Francisco. While that secrecy is frustrating for those of us interested in how uber-rich and politically powerful tech titans see the future of our world, it’s also rather savvy — no surprise from the guy who started hugely successful ventures like PayPal and Palantir. “It’s a pretty good marketing shtick if you want everybody to hear about something, not to let anybody in the room,” Thiel reportedly told one San Francisco audience last fall.

In March, he traveled to Rome for another private, four-part series on the Antichrist. Taking his shtick to the doorstep of the Vatican was guaranteed to generate publicity, and it did.

Months ago, recordings of Thiel’s lectures were leaked to The Verge. We have listened to and read transcripts of all four of these lectures, which provide a window into Thiel’s dizzying religious and sociocultural philosophy. He comes off as an intellectual magpie who somehow combines disparate elements into grave warnings against the AI and general “safetyism” that he claims precedes the Antichrist.

“Peace and safety” — the slogan of the Antichrist, according to Thiel — trouble him throughout the lectures. In the first, he wonders if we’re headed toward World War III or Cold War II, and afterward, potentially, an unjust peace, the corollary to an unjust war:

Somehow, it’s very strange how the first Cold War from ’49 to ’89 ended. But it ended with roughly what I think of as a just peace. Where somehow you didn’t have a nuclear war. And somehow our side, which I think was more the good side, basically won. And you ended up not with a perfect peace, but more or less a just peace. And so if we have World War III, it will be an unjust war. If we have Cold War II, maybe it can end in a just peace or an unjust peace.

Reflecting on this material and thinking about it, it’s obviously not written in stone and there’s a lot of different ways this stuff can go. But I keep thinking that, if you had to put odds on it, aren’t the odds that we’re trending towards the fourth quadrant this time? The fourth possibility is that Cold War II will end an unjust peace. And it’s because the Antichrist talks about Armageddon nonstop. We’re all scared to death that we’re sleepwalking into Armageddon. And then because we know World War III will be an unjust war, that pushes us very hard towards peace at any price.

What I worry about in that sort of situation is you don’t think too hard about the details of the peace and it becomes much more likely that you get an unjust peace. This is, by the way, the slogan of the Antichrist: 1 Thessalonians 5:3. It’s “peace and safety,” the unjust peace. And then what Christ says in Matthew 24:6, the full verse: “And you shall hear of wars and rumours of wars, see that ye be not troubled.” If you’re too troubled, will we always end up with very unjust peace? Or something like this.

We are publishing an analysis of these lectures now because Thiel published a version of these same ideas in the conservative religious journal First Things in July. You can read along for yourself. Titled “The Pope and the Antichrist,” the essay fills in the huge gaps in Thiel’s thinking and allows us to better understand his ideas, such as they are.

The bottom line is that after sifting through all of the arcane references and esoteric exegesis, it turns out that Thiel — a Protestant who likes to describe himself as a “heterodox Christian” — offers a fairly standard-issue American evangelical worldview, and a rather fundamentalist one at that.

He’s less a coherent religious thinker than a repackager of recognizable ideas — dressing them up in the rhetoric of a tech nerd turned theological hobbyist — which he uses to promote his own ideology. He reads everything from the Bible to pre-papal writings of a future pope to Robert Hugh Benson’s 1907 novel Lord of the World to semi-obscure Scottish poetry with an eye toward his own, sometimes shockingly literal interpretation of the Antichrist’s arrival (ideally, he should make his mark, as it were, more quickly than Jesus, who died at 33 and a few months — although Thiel allows in his third lecture that perhaps “in our gerontocracy, 66 is the new 33”). While his mashup of religious concepts and authoritative assertions on dubious interpretations make him sound like an undergrad who just took his first philosophy class and then a few too many hits on the bong, the goal of his eschatology is the same as every apocalyptic visionary: to divide the world between the saved and the damned. And Thiel is, clearly, one of the righteous.

It’s notable here that Thiel is coming from the heart of what is arguably America’s latest, and most unexpected, religious revival — one concentrated among the Silicon Valley elite, like the ACTS 17 Collective, which is a reference to St. Paul’s preaching to the Greek pagans in the Acts of the Apostles and an acronym for “Acknowledging Christ in Technology and Society.” But that movement presents an upbeat message of self-improvement through Jesus, the kind that the clean-and-fit Bay Area crowd tends to embrace. Thiel’s worldview is quite unusual for Silicon Valley, and perhaps especially unexpected for a gay German billionaire; he’s right at home in the US tradition of apocalypticism.

The key to Thiel’s theological vision comes at the very opening of his most recent First Things essay, and it is his fixation on, and fear of, the Antichrist. The Antichrist has traditionally been associated with, as Thiel himself put it elsewhere, “an evil king or tyrant or anti-messiah who appears in the end times.” That is true, though Thiel says that the Antichrist interests him “mostly because nobody else is talking about it.” That would be news to anybody with even a passing familiarity with American Christianity.

In fact, the Antichrist and eschatology are arguably the central religious impulse running through American Christianity, and that focus distinguishes the US from most other churches and cultures around the globe. In America, biblical teachings tend to jump from the Ten Commandments at the beginning of the Old Testament to the Book of Revelation at the end of the New Testament. The Gospels, the Beatitudes, all that provides the key teachings of Jesus Christ is a footnote.

The enthusiasm for the end of the world has been fueled in large part by the series of sweeping revivals, or “Great Awakenings,” that have marked American religious history from the Colonial era up through the 1800s and, some would say, on into the 20th century. These revivals focused not only on personal conversion but on dark warnings about the “end times” as foretold in the New Testament, when Christ would return to gather believers up to Heaven and those who remained would be stuck facing various tribulations on their own.

For American Christians especially, the quest to save souls from eternal damnation was increasingly driven by the fear that the Second Coming was imminent, so you’d better repent now. New apocalyptic movements and sects and cults continued to flourish, from those early tent revivals through the more slickly branded televangelists and, later, the enormously popular Left Behind series of novels in the 1990s. Forecasters variously took snippets in the Book of Daniel and other prophets in the Hebrew Bible and joined them with the often phantasmagoric array of visions from the Book of Revelation, and eventually what had been a confusing jumble of end times scenarios solidified into a widely accepted timeline: increasing natural and human-made disasters, the Second Coming of Jesus, aka the Rapture of true believers, followed by the rise of the Antichrist and seven years of the Great Tribulation on Earth, ending with a final battle between good and evil and a thousand years of peace.

“One of my friends was telling me that I should not pass up on the opportunity to tell those people in San Francisco that Bill Gates is the Antichrist. I will concede that he is certainly a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde-type character. The public Mr. Rogers, the neighborhood character — but I saw the Mr. Hyde version about a year ago, where it was just a nonstop Tourette’s, yelling swear words, almost incomprehensible what was going on. Certainly, of course, there are a lot of people who are wannabe Antichrists. They sort of want peace and safety. [He] definitely wants a Nobel Peace Prize. He would give his soul for that, no question about it.”

“There is another book — I haven’t been able to get a copy of it because it’s coming out tomorrow, but we sort of downloaded it — that fits this thesis even better. It’s from the East Bay rationalist Eliezer Yudkowsky. I’m embarrassed about all the ways I was once affiliated with these various people and how deranged and crazy they’ve all gone. It started with these Baconian aspirations of transformative technology: We’re going to build it, it’s going to change the world. And then it’s somehow ended in some sort of blackpilled thing that’s probably more depressed and more Luddite than Greta.”

“I think one of the ways these things always get reported is I denounce Greta as an Antichrist. And I want to be very clear, Greta is not, I mean, she’s maybe sort of a type or a shadow of an Antichrist of the sort that would be tempting, but I don’t want to flatter her too much.”

“It’s not Andreessen, by the way. I think Andreessen is not the Antichrist. Because, you know, the Antichrist is popular.”

Phew. Now enter Peter Thiel. He is in effect the latest in a long line of apocalypticists, though his own spin is that anxieties over strange new technologies like AI will prompt demands for greater regulation and that would be a grave, almost apocalyptic, mistake. Given the latest warnings from AI leaders themselves that the new technology could risk human extinction within a decade, Thiel’s concerns run counter to what you’d expect from an apocalypticist.

Thiel’s theological justification for criticizing this instinct toward what he derides as “safetyism” rests on a verse in St. Paul’s first letter to the Thessalonians in which the apostle warns that many will promote “peace and safety” to lull people into a false sense of security and then POOF, Jesus returns and the Antichrist appears and unbelievers are doomed.

Thiel identifies promoters of this kind of peace and safety with a “restraining” force that will be a sign of the coming of the Antichrist and which will eventually pave the way for the Antichrist. He has pointed to Anthony Fauci as one example of such a “restrainer.” And now the apostles of effective altruism, with their concern for protecting as many people as possible, are in Thiel’s sights. Thiel uses the original Greek term for “the restrainer,” katechon, because of course he does. Deploying arcane terms is part of the mystery that gives apocalypticism its allure, and prophets their power.

So who is actually the Antichrist? Thiel at one point dismissed such speculations as “down-market” behavior, but he himself cannot resist weighing in. Viewing the Roman pontiff as the Antichrist or a collaborator with the Antichrist is a standard trope of end times theology, and in his First Things essay Thiel follows that tradition by suggesting that the late Pope Francis could have been the Antichrist. In previously leaked snippets of Thiel’s talks he has accused the current American pope, Leo XIV, of being a “Chinese communist agent” or, more recently, Beijing’s “useful idiot,” because he wants to regulate AI — all very Antichrist-adjacent behavior.

Thiel has a somewhat unusual relationship to the Catholic Church. True to the more anti-papist strains of his tradition, he worries that Pope Leo XIV is a “woke American pope” who will join with American liberals to create a tyrannical “Caesaro-Papist fusion.”

At the same time, the German-born Thiel’s record-breaking financial support propelled JD Vance, a relatively recent Catholic convert, to the US Senate and now a heartbeat away from the presidency. Thiel has also made a little-known Catholic literary theorist from France, René Girard, a spiritual guide for America’s political right — though only by completely inverting Girard’s famous teaching about the scapegoat mechanism by which a society eases internal divisions by blaming a single person or subgroup of people for their problems.

Thiel’s latest essay is also unusual, or inventive, in that rather than denouncing the papacy as the Whore of Babylon — a traditional fundamentalist Protestant trope drawn from a stark image in Revelation 17 — he tries to co-opt one pope, the late Benedict XVI, into his very American and Protestant worldview and against the papacy and the Catholic Church itself.

news.title_zh: 彼得蒂尔罗马讲座曝光：痛批有效利他主义与安全派阻碍创新
news.summary_zh: 彼得·蒂尔在罗马讲座音频中猛烈抨击有效利他主义与AI安全派，称其为反基督先驱并将盖茨比作海德先生

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 硅谷风险投资家彼得·蒂尔在罗马的一场未公开讲座录音被曝光，他在演讲中直言抨击当前由有效利他主义主导的AI安全阵营。蒂尔指责所谓的AI末日论和安全主义实质上是神学意义上的反基督先驱，甚至将比尔·盖茨形容为双重人格中的海德先生，并将AI安全学者埃利亚泽·尤德科夫斯基斥为比环保少女更极端的卢德主义者。此番言论背后，是蒂尔代表的技术加速主义资本阵营与安斯罗皮克等机构所推崇的AI伦理监管派之间日趋白热化的意识形态冲突。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Leaked audio from a private lecture series in Rome reveals billionaire venture capitalist Peter Thiel launching a scathing attack on Effective Altruism (EA) and AI safetyism, casting them as theological forerunners to the Antichrist. Thiel labeled Bill Gates as 'Mr. Hyde' and ridiculed AI safety theorist Eliezer Yudkowsky as more Luddite than Greta Thunberg, escalating the ideological clash between techno-accelerationism and regulatory safetyism.

elements_zh.who: 硅谷传奇投资人彼得·蒂尔（Peter Thiel）
elements_zh.where: 意大利罗马举行的闭门讲座
elements_zh.what: 炮轰有效利他主义（EA）与AI安全派，称其为阻碍创新的卢德分子和反基督前驱，点名讽刺比尔·盖茨和尤德科夫斯基
elements_zh.why: 抵制以AI末日论为借口的严厉监管，为技术加速主义与资本无边界扩张抢夺舆论与道德高地

elements_en.who: Peter Thiel, venture capitalist and billionaire entrepreneur
elements_en.what: Lambasted Effective Altruism and AI safety advocates as apocalyptic anti-tech Luddites, comparing Gates to Mr. Hyde
elements_en.why: Pushing back against tightening AI regulatory overreach to defend techno-accelerationist capitalism

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 硅谷顶级富豪吵架的尽头原来也是跳大神。一边把拯救人类包装成禁欲系神教，另一边直接掏出圣经指责对方是反基督魔鬼；说到底，大家争的哪是什么人类未来，无非是到底该由谁来决定算力印钞机归谁管的权力游戏罢了。
ai_analysis.insight_en: When Silicon Valley's tech oligarchs clash, even existential risk arguments devolve into apocalyptic theology. Behind all the lofty talk of saving humanity or spotting the Antichrist, it's just two factions bickering over who gets the master key to the AI printing press.

news.content_snippet: Nvidia is in talks to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in Australian AI cloud provider Firmus, which abruptly pulled its initial public offering early …
news.summary_en: Nvidia is in advanced discussions to invest hundreds of millions of dollars into Australian AI cloud provider Firmus. The potential lifeline comes shortly after Firmus abruptly withdrew its initial public offering earlier this month, citing market volatility. The deal highlights Nvidia's ongoing playbook of deploying strategic capital to anchor demand for its AI hardware ecosystem across regional data centers.

The potential lifeline comes shortly after Firmus abruptly withdrew its initial public offering earlier this month, citing market volatility. The deal highlights Nvidia's ongoing playbook of deploying strategic capital to anchor demand for its AI hardware ecosystem across regional data centers.

news.article_content:

SpaceX alum’s aviation startup, Reliable Robotics, lands $115M, topping $1B valuation																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Kirsten Korosec
	

									
									
								
					
					
						6:17 AM PDT · October 20, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
Reliable Robotics has been working for nearly a decade to commercialize autonomous flying technology that can be installed on existing aircraft. Now, with a $115 million funding boost, the Mountain View, California-based startup has a longer runway as it pushes to get its autonomous flight system certified by the Federal Aviation Administration — a critical milestone that co-founder and CEO Robert Rose said the startup is inching toward.

The financing is an extension of its Series D round and includes $90 million in equity funding led by Nimble Partners and $25 million in debt from Silicon Valley Bank. The Series D round, which now totals $275 million, has pushed the startup’s valuation beyond the $1 billion mark. Other investors include Gideon Strategic Partners, RockCreek, Geek Ventures, Gold Hill Capital, Sparkwave Capital, and others. Reliable has raised $380 million to date.

“We continue to make steady progress and deliver evidence to the FAA and every day, we inch closer and closer,” said Rose, a former director of flight software at SpaceX who has also had stints at Tesla and Google. Reliable co-founder and CTO Juerg Frefel is also a SpaceX veteran who spent nearly a decade there as an engineer.

And in aviation — one of the most regulated industries in the world — moving toward certification of new technology is progress.

Reliable Robotics is working to gain FAA certification on four fronts, all of which are linked to its goal of autonomous flight.

Its first product, called continuous autopilot engagement, handles the engine startup, taxiing, takeoff, and landing for the pilot, who remains in the aircraft and interacts with the autonomous flight system through a touchscreen. Rose expects to receive certification for this critical first system in 18 to 24 months.

The second certification, which Rose says is at least three years away, removes the pilot from the cockpit and moves them to a ground-control station.

Reliable is also working toward certification of a collision-avoidance radar, which the company has developed in-house after failing to attract legacy suppliers to take on the project. Most conventional radar systems use an antenna that moves to scan the surrounding airspace. Reliable has developed a solid-state radar that has no moving parts and scans the sky at a longer range and at much higher resolution, according to Rose. It’s also easier to maintain because there are no moving parts and it costs less, he added.

“This is of great interest to operators these days, given the collisions that we’ve had recently in commercial aviation,” he said, adding that the radar also works on the ground to prevent collisions with other aircraft or infrastructure. Rose expects the solid-state radar to be certified by the end of 2027.

The final certification is for its airline, called Reliable Airlines, which will be the first airline certified to use the autonomous flying technology. The airline is based in Albuquerque and uses six Cessna Caravans — workhorses of the aviation industry — to fly cargo six days a week. (The FAA certifies equipment, but the agency also must certify the airline operations under a separate set of regulations.)

While the certification process is lengthy, Nimble Partners founder John Burbank said the benefits will be broad and significant.

“It’s a much bigger effort and much bigger opportunity than to just build one plane,” Burbank said, noting that Reliable is building a system that can be adopted by any airframe. “They had a really big vision nine years ago, and saw this as something needed and essential. Once they get the first one approved, then everyone will realize this is going to be the path for the industry, just as we’re seeing the path for the auto industry being autonomous.”

news.summary_en: Reliable Robotics, a developer of autonomous flight systems for retrofitting existing aircraft, has secured a $115 million extension to its Series D round, elevating its valuation past the $1 billion unicorn threshold. The round comprises $90 million in equity led by Nimble Partners alongside $25 million in venture debt. The fresh capital will extend the company's operational runway to achieve critical FAA airworthiness certification for commercial unmanned operations.
news.title_zh: 自动驾驶飞行商可靠机器人完成逾亿美元融资晋身独角兽
news.summary_zh: 可靠机器人公司完成1.15亿美元D轮延期融资，估值破10亿美元并加速民航适航认证

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 致力于研发飞机自动驾驶改装系统的可靠机器人公司完成1.15亿美元的D轮延期融资，其中包括9000万美元股权融资与2500万美元债权融资，助推其投后估值正式突破10亿美元大关。这家由前航天技术团队创立的企业历经近十年技术研发，旨在为现有存量飞机加装全自主飞行系统。本轮资金将主要用于支持其自动驾驶系统通过美国联邦航空管理局的适航适规认证，以推进商业货运航线落地。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Reliable Robotics, a developer of autonomous flight systems for retrofitting existing aircraft, has secured a $115 million extension to its Series D round, elevating its valuation past the $1 billion unicorn threshold. The round comprises $90 million in equity led by Nimble Partners alongside $25 million in venture debt. The fresh capital will extend the company's operational runway to achieve critical FAA airworthiness certification for commercial unmanned operations.

news.title: An interview with OnlyFans CEO Keily Blair about plans to offer financial services to its 2.5M active creators, a potential IPO, and more (Emma Hinchliffe/Fortune)
news.title_en: An interview with OnlyFans CEO Keily Blair about plans to offer financial services to its 2.5M active creators, a potential IPO, and more (Emma Hinchliffe/Fortune)
news.author: Fortune
news.article_content:
That’s why we had OnlyFans’ current CEO, Keily Blair, onstage at the Fortune Most Powerful Women Summit last week. I interviewed Blair onstage about her vision for the future of OnlyFans, which is at the precipice of a brand-new chapter.

Earlier this year, OnlyFans’ very private owner, Leonid Radvinsky, died of cancer in his 40s. After his death, the company brought on a firm called Architect Capital as its first institutional investor. With Architect, OnlyFans is now crafting a new vision of what the company can be.

The first major change on its roadmap is to begin offering financial services products to the 2.5 million active creators on the platform. Many of those creators make explicit content, and are thus often rejected by mainstream banks. Financial institutions are fearful of facilitating crimes like sex trafficking and paint with a broad brush. Even Blair herself has been rejected by a bank for serving as OnlyFans’ CEO; at one point, OnlyFans itself almost got cut off from mainstream financial services, threatening the future of its business and leading its original founders to sell.

Blair says that OnlyFans can offer banking products where mainstream institutions can’t because it has more information about its creators. “We have full visibility into the content that’s being created,” she told me. “There’s a huge difference between perceived risk and actual risk.”

And yet the risk is still real. I was shaken reading more this year about the details of the Tate brothers’ trafficking operation, which involved trafficking women into creating content for OnlyFans and training other men to do the same. I asked Blair what goes through her mind when she hears about such things happening on the platform she leads. “It’s horrific,” she told me.

OnlyFans is already one of the most successful tech companies to come out of the U.K. It did $1.55 billion in revenue in 2025, its 20% cut of $7.85 billion processed on the platform that year. In addition to financial services products, OnlyFans is also aiming to get more into mainstream entertainment—as AI microdramas proliferate across social media, could OnlyFans help creators produce their own?—and offer its own version of algorithmic discovery for the first time. OnlyFans has traditionally required users to find their preferred creators on other platforms like X and Reddit, and then track down their OnlyFans accounts, rather than recommend content to users. The fear is recommending explicit content to someone who doesn’t wish to see it; OnlyFans just began testing discovery in the Netherlands, Blair told me, and will trial in more markets.

All of this lays the groundwork for a possible OnlyFans IPO. The closest precedent would be Reddit’s 2024 IPO, Blair says. “It’s a social media platform with a high concentration of adult content,” she explains.

She didn’t have any news to announce, but confirmed a public offering is on the agenda. “We’re thinking about that pathway towards an IPO and working toward that as a potential goal for the company,” she says.

Women over 50 are the group most opposed to data centers. According to a survey by Bryson Gillette. Sixty-six percent of women oppose a data center being built in their community, vs. 50% of men. Among those 50+, that's 72% and 58%.

GM's challenges are 'intensifying.' So says CEO Mary Barra, No. 2 on the 2026 Fortune Most Powerful Women list. The automaker just cut the high end of its forecast and saw its share price drop, even while beating expectations for the quarter.

Melania Trump is the latest voice for women's health. President Trump yesterday signed an executive order creating a Women’s Health Division at the National Institutes of Health and a separate White House Women’s Health Task Force. The order doesn't come with any new funding. The first lady was reportedly the one to push for the priority and made the announcement.

About that Poppi exit. PepsiCo acquired the prebiotic soda brand for close to $2 billion last year, promising an additional $300 million for founders Allison and Stephen Ellsworth if the brand met certain benchmarks. In December, the company was projecting Poppi would earn $278 million of that—but last week cut its earnout to just $12 million.

"I think about perception all the time. It’s a big part of my job. It’s not cool at all."

news.title: Google says it is rolling out Personal Intelligence for Gemini on Android Auto now and to cars with Google built-in in the coming months as an opt-in feature (Abner Li/9to5Google)
news.title_en: Google says it is rolling out Personal Intelligence for Gemini on Android Auto now and to cars with Google built-in in the coming months as an opt-in feature (Abner Li/9to5Google)
news.author: 9to5Google
news.article_content:
Like in the Gemini app or AI Mode, Personal Intelligence taps into your Google Workspace (including Gmail and Calendar), Photos, Maps, Search, and YouTube to personalize responses. Your prompts and commands don’t have to include specifics as Personal Intelligence can pull those details from emails, photos, or a “place you saved in Google Maps.”

This allows for complex or natural queries, like “What’s my flight gate? And is my flight on time?” or “Take me to my doctor’s appointment.”

Additionally, Gemini is aware of your preferences when you say: “Find me an indoor restaurant along my route that matches my usual vibe.” This saves you from having to specify you’re vegetarian with every command.

On the privacy front, Personal Intelligence is opt-in, though it will come to Android Auto automatically if you enabled it for the Gemini app on your phone.

If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you.

Meanwhile, on Android Automotive, Personal Intelligence will only share personalized responses “when you’re in the car with your phone connected.”

Personal Intelligence is rolling out starting today to Android Auto, with Android Automotive availability in the coming months.

news.title: PHP development team plans to release updates tomorrow to address two vulnerabilities, each rated 9.2; security researchers at watchTowr say they are RCE flaws (Lawrence Abrams/BleepingComputer)
news.title_en: PHP development team plans to release updates tomorrow to address two vulnerabilities, each rated 9.2; security researchers at watchTowr say they are RCE flaws (Lawrence Abrams/BleepingComputer)
news.author: BleepingComputer
news.article_content:

The PHP security team is warning administrators to prepare for emergency security updates tomorrow to address two critical vulnerabilities, as information about the flaws has reportedly leaked ahead of their scheduled disclosure.

PHP powers many websites and web applications, including content management systems, e-commerce platforms, and custom web services.

In an advisory published Tuesday, the PHP development team announced that it plans to release security updates on Wednesday, October 21, at 14:00 UTC (10:00 AM Eastern), to address two vulnerabilities, each rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0.

The PHP security team also sent a notice to its ANNOUNCE mailing list, urging administrators to prepare to install the security updates as soon as they become available.

"We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild," the PHP security team warned.

The developers have not disclosed any technical details about the vulnerabilities, including which PHP versions are affected, how they can be exploited, or which releases will contain fixes.

However, security researchers at watchTowr told BleepingComputer that the vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are remote code execution (RCE) flaws believed to affect PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8.

"In the last hour, two remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP have been leaked. These vulnerabilities were previously scheduled under embargo and due for release on Thursday at 11 am ET," watchTowr CEO Benjamin Harris told BleepingComputer.

"While we are not able to share technical information at this point for obvious reasons, given the sensitivity, we can confirm that these vulnerabilities are indeed real. Both of them are CVSS10 and are understood to affect PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8."

watchTowr also said it believes it has successfully reproduced CVE-2026-109618 but is not releasing technical information until security patches become available.

The researchers clarified that they have not observed exploitation of the vulnerabilities in the wild, despite the information reportedly leaking ahead of the planned disclosure.

In a post on X, watchTowr warned that information about the vulnerabilities had leaked before the originally planned disclosure date.

"We were all supposed to wait until Thursday at 11am ET. Information has leaked wrt zero-day embargoed RCE vulns in PHP. We can confirm that they're real," the researchers said.

The warning follows a now-deleted post on Y Combinator's Hacker News forum, in which a user named "petecooper" claimed that two critical PHP remote code execution vulnerabilities would be disclosed on October 22.

The post, seen by BleepingComputer, claimed that both vulnerabilities carried CVSS scores of 10.0 and affected PHP versions dating back to PHP 5.

It also identified the vulnerabilities as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, matching the identifiers watchTowr later shared.

However, watchTowr's statements and the Hacker News post are different from PHP's official announcement. Both described the vulnerabilities as CVSS 10.0, while the PHP security team assigned each a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2.

Additionally, watchTowr cited an originally planned Thursday disclosure, while PHP has officially scheduled its security release for tomorrow morning.

The PHP security team says it will publish full technical details, affected versions, and fixed releases when the security updates become available.

Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a possible merger, Elon Musk said during the latter’s third quarter earnings call Tuesday.

Musk, who serves as CEO of both companies, said the special committees were formed at the request of shareholders and consist of independent directors (though he did not name them). He also noted that he is not a member of either committee, nor involved in any of the discussions.

“Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees,” Musk said. “So it’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking and I can’t be in the conversation.”

The groups have not reached agreement on the terms of any transaction — and there’s no guarantee that they will. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this,” he continued. “And particularly on the Tesla side, we will need a 50 percent vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders. And that’s quite a high hurdle to try to achieve.”

That said, Musk called the possibility of a Tesla-SpaceX merger a “good idea.” He continued:

I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity. And there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the TeraFab, obviously robotics, mass to orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity. So I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies. They’ve got to come up with something and then that’s going to be put to the shareholders as a vote.

A Tesla-SpaceX merger would be a blockbuster corporate deal creating a mega-entity valued upwards of $3.6 trillion. But combining Musk’s car and energy company with his AI and rocket company would not be without its tradeoffs. A lot depends on which company absorbs the other. To buy SpaceX, Tesla would have to create millions of new stock shares, which for current Tesla owners would mean owning a smaller slice of a much larger pie. SpaceX’s launch goals require tens of billions of dollars every year — extra spending that could drain Tesla’s ability to build new car factories and battery plants.

That said, most Wall Street analysts and legal experts believe SpaceX would acquire Tesla (or absorb it through a stock swap) rather than vice versa. Since its IPO, SpaceX has maintained a higher valuation than Tesla. A merger in that direction would allow SpaceX shareholders to hold the majority control of the combined mega-entity. Some Tesla shareholders may balk at this deal.

But it would also create one company for those who believe in Musk’s vision of the future — robot cars, humanoid robots, AI super-intelligence, and human habitats on Mars — in which to place their investments. And Tesla shareholder approved Musk’s enormous pay package last year — even after a Delaware judge tossed it over lack of independence.

Earlier this month, Barclays published a client note suggesting a potential Tesla-SpaceX combination could be announced ahead of Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting scheduled for December 3, 2026.

news.title: It’s a bird, it’s a plane … it’s a robo-puffin?
news.title_en: It’s a bird, it’s a plane … it’s a robo-puffin?
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume. Yet birds like gulls and puffins can plunge into the sea, swim underwater, and leap back into the air to fly away. And now engineers at MIT and EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, have designed a robot that can do likewise.

The “flapping-wing aerial-aquatic vehicle,” or FAAV, weighs less than 300 grams (about half a pound) and is equipped with a central fuselage, two flexible wings, and a steerable tail. The body contains a battery and a waterproof electric motor that drives a crankshaft, which pumps the wings up and down at preset frequencies. The wings are made of thin membranes that are coated with hydrophobic nanoparticles to help wick away water. And the tail is motorized, enabling it to change its angle to help the robot fly up or dive down.

In experiments carried out in a water tank and at Lake Geneva, a team led by Raphael Zufferey, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, identified combinations of wing size, flapping frequency, and tail angle that enable the robot to smoothly transition from swimming to flying.

news.title: Here’s the tea
news.title_en: Here’s the tea
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
When Tristan Brown, an associate professor of history at MIT, first examined a Chinese tea chest label displayed at Old South Meeting House, he had no reason to doubt its story. Descendants of the Boston blacksmith Thomas Wells had donated the label in 1987, saying it had been recovered after colonial protesters threw tea into Boston Harbor in 1773.

But after a year of research, Brown reached a different conclusion: The label was made nearly a century later. The decisive clue came when he read the Chinese text in Cantonese rather than Mandarin, as previous scholars had done. He found that the characters had been used phonetically, in slightly variant forms across contemporary sources, to represent the name of Smith, Archer & Co., a US firm that acquired Asian tea for shipment to American markets during the 1860s and 1870s.

Working with the Wells family, he traced the label to a relative who traveled from Michigan to California during the Gold Rush era before returning and operating a business known as the California Tea Store. Brown argues that claims for its revolutionary pedigree probably developed later, amid the centennial commemorations of the 1870s.

news.title: Melt it, spin it, use it again
news.title_en: Melt it, spin it, use it again
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
The average American throws out around 81 pounds of clothing each year, and there are few options for recycling it. MIT engineers hope to cut down on that textile waste with a new type of yarn.

The thermoplastic yarn mimics the properties of conventional elastic yarns, which typically combine spandex with polyester or nylon. Those fibers would have to be separated for recycling—a process that isn’t practical. But the MIT team found a way to create a similarly stretchy yarn from two variations of polyethylene, a material commonly used in milk jugs and grocery bags. Because they come from the same chemical family, the yarn can be melted as is. news.title: A reason to eat carbs
news.title_en: A reason to eat carbs
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
A high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet can help some people lose weight, and some research has shown that it may protect against colon cancer. But a new study suggests that such a ketogenic diet may also increase the risk of cancer in the small intestine.

This type of diet forces the body to burn fatty acids instead of carbohydrates for fuel, producing by-products called ketone bodies. One of these, BHB, was thought to be responsible for the protective effect observed against colon cancer.

Omer Yilmaz, director of the MIT Stem Cell Initiative, worked with colleagues including MIT postdocs Jessica Shay and Fangtao Chi to investigate whether the effects were similar in the small intestine. But instead, they found that mice on a ketogenic diet were more likely to develop tumors in that part of the gastrointestinal system than those on a control diet were.

The findings cast serious doubt on treating keto as a risk-free metabolic panacea.

news.title: Robotic therapy for stroke patients
news.title_en: Robotic therapy for stroke patients
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
Strokes leave 5 million people with long-term impairments each year, and a growing shortage of physical therapists makes it hard for them to get the care they need. A new approach tries to solve that problem by combining artificial intelligence and human therapy.

Johannes Lachner, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Purdue University, and Noah Geiger, a former visiting student at MIT, developed a robotic system that uses generative AI and real-time force feedback to learn from real therapists. Drawing on what it’s learned, it gives patients just the right amount of assistance during physical rehabilitation exercises like reaching, lifting their arms, and performing tasks of daily living.

The goal is “not to replace therapists, but to extend their reach,” Lachner says.
news.original_content:
Strokes leave 5 million people with long-term impairments each year, and a growing shortage of physical therapists makes it hard for them to get the care they need. A new approach tries to solve that problem by combining artificial intelligence and human therapy.

Johannes Lachner, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Purdue University, and Noah Geiger, a former visiting student at MIT, developed a robotic system that uses generative AI and real-time force feedback to learn from real therapists. Drawing on what it’s learned, it gives patients just the right amount of assistance during physical rehabilitation exercises like reaching, lifting their arms, and performing tasks of daily living.

The goal is “not to replace therapists, but to extend their reach,” Lachner says.

news.title: Taking a swing at a pickleball startup
news.title_en: Taking a swing at a pickleball startup
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
In corporate America, Stanley Anderson ’79 says, executives often assume that their peers grew up in privileged circumstances.

“I spent my early years trying not to get recruited into gangs, getting shot at, watching my friends get murdered, and thinking that if I don’t leave, I will die,” says Anderson, who was raised in Chicago. “I was fortunate to survive.”

But he thrived, building an impressive career at the likes of HP, Intel, and the Palo Alto Research Center. Now he is applying his management expertise as CEO of Costa Pickleball, a Las Vegas–based startup that sells high-performance paddles in decorative designs. Beyond giving customers a way to, as he says, “bring their identity to the court,” he is also betting on technology: He’s developing a quieter type of paddle he expects will provide a competitive advantage.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 曾任职于惠普、英特尔及施乐帕洛阿尔托研究中心（PARC）的资深硅谷黑人高管斯坦利·安德森，出任拉斯维加斯初创企业Costa Pickleball首席执行官。凭借从芝加哥帮派暴力街区逆袭至科技高层的独特背景，他将企业硬核工程管理方法引入当下火热的匹克球运动，主打兼具视觉个性与高性能的球拍产品。针对欧美社区普遍抗议的匹克球高分贝击球噪音问题，其团队正押注新型声学材料技术，研发具备绝对竞争优势的专利静音球拍。

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 科技老兵降维打击消费品的套路总是惊人一致：先讲一段九死一生的励志童年，再把给芯片做封装的热学、声学实验室经验，拿来给中产阶级的拍子消音。只要能解决社区大妈投诉噪音，这门玄学就值大钱。

If it stops neighbors calling the cops, people will gladly pay a 300% markup.

news.summary_en: SpaceX reported a massive Q3 capital expenditure of $19.6B, nearly tripling from $6.9B a year earlier, while its connectivity revenue—primarily driven by Starlink—surged 69% year-over-year to $5.2B. The unprecedented capex surge reflects heavy investments in rocket cadence, Starlink constellations, and AI-era compute infrastructure.

news.title: SpaceX reports Q3 revenue up 161% YoY to $14.58B, vs. $12.72B est., AI revenue up 830% to $7.56B, and AI operating income of $431M, up from a loss of $1.7B (Lora Kolodny/CNBC)
news.title_en: SpaceX reports Q3 revenue up 161% YoY to $14.58B, vs. $12.72B est., AI revenue up 830% to $7.56B, and AI operating income of $431M, up from a loss of $1.7B (Lora Kolodny/CNBC)
news.author: CNBC
news.article_content:
This is CNBC's live coverage of SpaceX's 2026 third-quarter earnings.

SpaceX reported 161% revenue growth for the third quarter, beating Wall Street estimates, as the company's artificial intelligence business grew ninefold. The stock rose about 1.5% in extended trading on Tuesday.

Here's how the company did compared to LSEG consensus estimates:

It's not immediately clear if the reported earnings are comparable to the LSEG analyst estimate.

SpaceX said in a release that it recorded operating income of $2.8 billion and net income of $4.4 billion. In the same period a year earlier, SpaceX reported a net loss of $1.05 billion.

While SpaceX is best known for its reusable rockets, most of its revenue and profit in recent quarters came from the company's connectivity segment, which consists of its Starlink satellite internet service.

Buzz has been building about Starlink's plans to build a U.S. mobile network after SpaceX, earlier this month, announced that it's buying 800 MHz of low-band spectrum, and after the Federal Communications Commission approved a plan for the company to build out a 15,000-satellite constellation.

SpaceX jumped into AI with the purchase earlier this year of xAI, which was Elon Musk's AI lab. The company has been rapidly expanding that business by renting out capacity to Google, Anthropic and others.

AI, which the company now calls "Super Intelligence," has emerged as SpaceX's largest business. Revenue jumped ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the same quarter last year. Analysts expected sales of $6.47 billion, according to StreetAccount.

During the third quarter, SpaceX also closed its $60 billion purchase of AI coding startup Cursor.

Meanwhile, SpaceX's launch business was up just slightly in the quarter, with sales rising to $1.77 billion from $1.67 billion a year ago.

SpaceX is scheduled to hold its third-quarter earnings call at 4:30 p.m. ET. The company encouraged shareholders to submit questions online ahead of the meeting.

Musk's other public company, Tesla, is scheduled to post third-quarter results on Wednesday. Analysts expect revenue at the electric vehicle maker to dip slightly from a year ago to $27.9 billion, according to LSEG.

Tesla shares are down about 17% this year as of Tuesday, leaving the company with a market cap of almost $1.5 billion.

CoreWeave and Nebius in OctoberSpaceX is relatively new to the cloud computing business. Many of its competitors in the space, the so-called neoclouds, have been getting hammered on Wall Street of late on concerns that rising interest rates are going to make the costly buildout financially burdensome.

CoreWeave and Nebius are down 28% so far in October, while IREN has plunged about 35%. Earlier this month, Australian AI data center operator Firmus withdrew its planned IPO, citing market volatility and conditions.

While SpaceX is far less reliant on that side of its business than are the neoclouds, capital costs still matter, and the company is banking on the AI boom continuing. In the second quarter, debt and finance leases increased to $36.8 billion, up from $22 billion the prior period.

SpaceX stock chart.Since opening at $150 on June 12, SpaceX shares have edged slightly lower, slipping to $147.50 on Tuesday. That gives Space a market cap of about $2 trillion.

The stock hit a low of $104.83 on Aug. 3, a few days before the first post-IPO lockup expired, making more than 911 million SpaceX shares available for trading.

The lockup lifted on Aug. 6, and the stock rallied, popping 6% initially, then nearly 16% the day after.

SpaceX continues to serve as a critical launch provider to the U.S. Defense Department and NASA.

The business hasn't been historically profitable, but it's the segment that captured the public's interest in the rocket maker. In the second quarter, SpaceX reported launch revenue of $962 million and a net loss of $542 million.

Future profitability hinges on the success of SpaceX's Starship mega-rocket, which is still being developed and tested.

Since the company's last earnings call in August, SpaceX hit multiple milestones, reaching orbit and using Starship to deploy dozens of its new V.3 Starlink satellites during Test Flight 14. But the rocket is still far from reliable or reusable.

Investors are awaiting an update on pending NASA missions and the future of the older Falcon rocket. SpaceX has reportedly stopped allowing other companies to launch their cargo, including satellites, into orbit on Falcon missions.

In its first earnings report in August, SpaceX reported capital expenditures of $18.4 billion, with 80% of that going towards its artificial intelligence division.

That number spooked Wall Street, and shares dropped following the report.

SpaceX and xAI merged in February and the company has been pouring money into its effort to become a major player in AI, a market dominated by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. The AI division also acquired Cursor in a $60 billion transaction and is now known as either SpaceXAI or SpaceXSI, with the "SI" standing for President Donald Trump's preferred "Super Intelligence."

Wall Street is sounding bullish on SpaceX ahead of its third-quarter earnings report, to be delivered after the bell on Tuesday.

Mizuho has an outperform rating on the stock and a $200 price target, per a Monday note from analyst Brett Linzey. Shares were trading around $148 as of 10:45 a.m. on Tuesday.

news.title: Astrolab’s upcoming rover will run the first LLMs on the moon
news.title_en: Astrolab’s upcoming rover will run the first LLMs on the moon
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
Large language models are set to go lunar. A computer capable of running AI software is one of the payloads aboard Astrolab’s FLIP lunar rover, which is slated to head to Earth’s celestial companion as early as November 2026.

The 480-kilogram FLIP rover, short for “FLEX Lunar Innovation Platform,” is the first in a series of vehicles NASA’s contracted from Astrolab, including future buggies that will move Artemis astronauts across the moon’s surface. Fitted with deformable wheels engineered for the rugged terrain and designed to survive at least 150 hours of the frigid lunar night, FLIP will carry 20 scientific payloads including a lidar 3D mapper and a sensor to measure concentrations of the isotope helium-3 in lunar regolith.

The rover will also carry a high-performance computer made by HPE that will be the first to run LLMs on the moon’s surface. Such software could ultimately help enable greater autonomy and real-time intelligent decision-making in space on future missions, eliminating the time delays and limited bandwidth that often plague long-distance communications between ground control on Earth and robots elsewhere in the solar system.

news.title: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs
news.title_en: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs
news.author: Ars Technica
news.article_content:
Security personnel around the world are on high alert Tuesday following the discovery of eight TLS certificates with private keys so weak they could allow anyone to mint trusted browser and app credentials for any site on the Internet.

As of late morning Tuesday, browser makers and some major apps and programming languages had blocked all eight of the intermediate certificates. There are no reports of certificate transparency logs, which track the issuance of all browser-trusted certificates, showing the compromised keys being used maliciously. The threat remains far from over, however, because it will be hard and time-consuming to update other key parts of the Internet, such as Linux distributions and embedded and Internet of Things devices.

The eight intermediate certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra Limited. ai_analysis.briefing_en: Anthropic's latest draft IPO prospectus revealed that its H1 2026 revenue exploded to $16.3 billion, up almost fifteenfold from $1.1 billion in H1 2025, with roughly 20% concentrated in just two major customers. However, massive non-cash accounting adjustments and compute capital charges resulted in an eye-popping net paper loss of $80.7 billion for the six-month period.

news.title: A profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma; sources: Xbox plans a major Game Pass overhaul, a next-gen handheld device by late 2027, and next-gen console by late 2028 (Sebastian Herrera/Fortune)
news.title_en: A profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma; sources: Xbox plans a major Game Pass overhaul, a next-gen handheld device by late 2027, and next-gen console by late 2028 (Sebastian Herrera/Fortune)
news.author: Fortune
news.article_content:
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. MERON MENGHISTAB for FortuneBy Sebastian HerreraSebastian HerreraTech CorrespondentDown Arrow Button IconBy Sebastian HerreraSebastian HerreraTech CorrespondentDown Arrow Button IconOctober 20, 2026, 12:10 PM ETGoogle source logoAdd Fortune on Google for similar content.Add us on GoogleAdd us on GoogleAsha Sharma returns from one of her walking meetings around Microsoft’s sprawling campus in Redmond, Wash., to her relatively new office in the Xbox building, reached via a 1,100-foot-long bridge from the main offices. It’s a brisk early September afternoon, and Sharma is wading through the next series of changes she’ll make at the legacy gaming business. There are more layoffs to complete and more studios to consolidate.

Much is still new for Sharma, the 38-year-old executive whom Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella in February put in charge of turning around one of entertainment’s biggest brands. Her office, adorned with Xbox controllers, framed Halo game discs, and a Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater skateboard, at first seems like an odd fit for an executive who famously had zero past video game experience.

Yet the Xbox CEO who’s replaced gaming legend Phil Spencer is moving fast. Xbox’s finances have been in shambles while its market share has tanked from its peak years ago. Sharma must fix its economics while improving its brand. She has been blunt about Xbox’s poor performance; has cut thousands of staff members; is reimagining how Xbox markets and sells its products; is upending its tech stack; has divested or reorganized smaller studios; and is focusing Xbox around its biggest franchises and publishing groups, including Blizzard Entertainment.

If Spencer was a gamer’s gamer, Sharma is the decisive boardroom boss.

Only Xbox’s is a very big, and opinionated, board. Every gaming conference Sharma attends, every decision she makes, and every post she publishes on social media is being closely watched by rabid gaming fans and Microsoft’s top brass.

“It’s hard to be a first-time CEO … where everybody sees everything you do,” Sharma told Fortune, sitting in one of her office’s blue velvet chairs, with several packs of NeeDoh stress balls by her side and wedding invitations from fans on her desk. “We are trying to get done an inordinate amount of things in an inordinate amount of time.”

The attention, Sharma said, is a reflection of how much Xbox matters to people. “The benefit of everybody caring is that you’re going to be able to pick out things that people really care about to actually make our product better,” she said.

Unafraid to create tensions, the jacket- and sneaker-loving executive has come in clear-eyed and with swagger, indirectly questioning her predecessor’s strategy, and has shown a remarkable knack for marketing that plan with deftly written employee memos, new slogans, and strategic posts on social media, where meme after meme of Sharma also appear. (One deepfake video shows her yelling, “You’re all fired!” to a group of studio employees.)

Flashy moves aside, Sharma has a challenging road ahead. Turning around a sprawling $21 billion business that includes hardware, creative studios, and thousands of video game titles is a task that would test even the most experienced of CEOs. And at a time when Microsoft is intensely focused on competing in the AI race, many industry observers wonder how committed the company is to the gaming business, and if Nadella has put Sharma in charge to prepare for an eventual sale or spinoff.

For an enterprise software company like Microsoft, a consumer gaming business stands out as a bit of an “odd condiment,” said Joost van Dreunen, a gaming expert and professor at NYU’s Stern School of Business. “How you value, operate, manage, and finance a creative division is very different than most of the other parts of the Microsoft empire.”

As Sharma works to revitalize the storied gaming unit, Microsoft employees, investors, analysts, and gamers are all focused on a key question: Can a gaming industry outsider bring Xbox back to its glory days—and if she can, under what structure will that happen?

For all its current challenges, Xbox is a Microsoft success story. In the quarter-century since the software giant launched its first console, Xbox has grown into one of the company’s most visible and influential global consumer brands. Even if you’ve never picked up a game controller, there’s a good chance you recognize some of its hits.

There are cultural touchstones like Halo, a first-person shooter game that became a global multimedia franchise spanning a television series, comic books, and toys.

There’s Xbox Live, which helped make multiplayer online gaming a mainstream form of entertainment.

And there’s the beloved Xbox 360 console of the mid-2000s, which at its peak rivaled Sony’s PlayStation in sales, and on which a generation of young gamers—including this writer—cut their teeth.

With Microsoft’s 2023 acquisition of game publisher Activision Blizzard for $69 billion, Xbox gained custody of blockbuster titles like Call of Duty, World of Warcraft, and Overwatch, making it one of the most significant players in a video game market that has ballooned to several times the size of the global theatrical box office.

The fact that Xbox now finds itself in fix-it mode instead of on a victory tour for its 25-year milestone is the result of what current and former employees say has been a series of strategic miscalculations, conflicting internal priorities, and a loss of focus on the basics.

Game Pass, a Netflix-style monthly gaming service, helped Xbox build a subscription business. But it also led to a cannibalization of sales for the company’s higher-priced first-party game titles, especially during the critical launch period. And competing internal metrics within different teams—such as subscription revenue versus store revenue—exacerbated the problem, said former employees.

As Microsoft acquired more game publishers—including Minecraft-maker Mojang Studios—it didn’t pay enough attention to its core console, which still represents 80% of its business, former Xbox employees said. PlayStation and Nintendo have offered more exclusive titles that lock in gamers.

The Activision Blizzard acquisition, in particular, made the overall business more complex and intensified pressure to show returns. The purchase vaulted Xbox to become Microsoft’s third-largest business by revenue.

“If there’s any place that we got out of sync maybe in the last five years, it’s not that any one of those [individual bets] wasn’t working. It’s just that we hadn’t connected the dots maybe as well as we should have,” Matt Booty, Xbox’s chief content officer, told Fortune.

While Xbox remains one of the three major console platforms, it’s seen a big drop-off. Current-generation Xbox consoles have sold just a little over a third as many units as the PlayStation 5, according to third-party estimates. Higher hardware costs, fueled by memory chip shortages, are adding to the woes.

A Microsoft measure of profit margin has been around 3% for the Xbox unit, a third to a tenth of competitors’ levels and a far cry from the typical expectations Microsoft Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood has for its major businesses.

Sharma’s turnaround strategy is about focusing on hardware, player experience, high-value franchises, updating Xbox’s tech, and meeting gamers where they’re at.

“We’re not here to do the minimum viable thing to just have a good business,” she said. “We’re here to be the No. 1 entertainment company.”

Some of her vision is becoming clearer. Xbox is planning a major overhaul of Game Pass that would have players choose features à la carte, including add-ons for console-only games, cloud gaming, and multiplayer, with the system operating on a tiered structure, according to people familiar with the strategy. Sharma also plans to release a next-generation handheld device by the 2027 holiday season and the next console by the holidays in 2028.

Inside the company’s secretive lab, known as Building 87 on campus, she has been plotting with lead designers such as Carl Ledbetter about the next-gen Project Helix hardware that could get gamers to stick with Xbox for mobile play, tinkering in regular stand-up meetings over prototypes and which strategic partnerships might help Xbox evolve.

While she has a reputation for being blunt, she is also introverted. In meetings, she often sits back and listens, sometimes while on her phone, yet tracking every detail, stopping discussions to ask sharp, probing questions or offer direct feedback, staff members said. She’s often chewing gum, and she is known to call colleagues from her car to check in while on her morning commute.

“As a leader, you’re taught to be confident, and I think being curious is way more important,” Sharma said. “If you’re confident, you might be right, and if you’re curious, you will find a better way. If people understand what’s happening, they will come up with better ideas to fix it than anyone else will.”

Soon after her appointment as head of Xbox, Sharma traveled to Blizzard’s campus in Irvine, Calif., to get a sense of gaming culture and meet with Blizzard President Johanna Faries, who told Fortune that Sharma has led primarily through inquiry, asking a myriad of questions to understand how things are working.

news.summary_en: Following her appointment as head of Microsoft's gaming division, new Xbox CEO Asha Sharma is orchestrating a sweeping turnaround marked by studio consolidations, further layoffs, and an overhaul of the Game Pass subscription model. Insiders reveal a concrete hardware roadmap targeting a next-gen gaming handheld by late 2027 and a flagship next-gen home console by late 2028.

news.author: TechCrunch
news.article_content:

Google has joined Amazon in attacking Nvidia’s stronghold with AI app developers																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Julie Bort
	

									
									
								
					
					
						11:38 AM PDT · October 20, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
On Tuesday, Google announced that TorchTPU, its long-awaited version of PyTorch, is now available as an open-source project. With this, Google joins Amazon in trying to break Nvidia’s stranglehold on the AI industry, where most AI apps are written by default to run on Nvidia’s chips, or GPUs.

PyTorch is the popular open-source toolkit that AI app developers and startups use to build, train, and run AI models. It is, by some accounts, used by 85% of the AI apps. PyTorch was originally developed by Meta (then Facebook) in 2016, long before the world had an inkling that LLMs would change the world. At the time, Nvidia’s GPUs were already the standard hardware for AI research, so many of PyTorch’s features were built to work specifically with them. In 2022, Meta turned PyTorch over to the Linux Foundation, a nonprofit that manages many important open source projects.

Google’s version, TorchTPU, lets AI apps run on Google’s AI chips, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also makes it easy to move existing PyTorch apps to TPUs and, therefore, to Google Cloud. Developers can do this with a simple configuration change and no re-writing of their apps.

Amazon made a similar announcement Monday, when it released its own version of PyTorch, called TorchNeuron. TorchNeuron allows AI apps to be ported to Amazon’s homegrown AI chip, Trainium, and to AWS with no rewriting. Amazon also said it going even further in its effort to loosen Nvidia’s hold on PyTorch. It is submitting code to the main PyTorch project that decouples various features from Nvidia’s chips, making it more open to any hardware by default.

Google may be one-upping Amazon in a few ways, however. It says it worked directly with Meta, Hugging Face, Inferact (maker of vLLM) RadixArk (maker of SGLang), and others to ensure that TorchTPU’s features and code libraries work well with these popular AI development tools, just as the original PyTorch does.

Plus the search giant has launched a dedicated tool, the TPU agent suite, to help developers move their apps to Google’s chips and cloud and fix errors along the way. It even updated its popular LiteRT tool, which runs AI on phones, laptops and embedded devices, to work better with PyTorch AI apps.

None of this means AI app developers will automatically ditch Nvidia’s hardware en masse just because they can now easily move to alternative chips and clouds. But Amazon and Google are clearly working to end Nvidia’s advantage.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 全球人工智能领军企业完成了对专注药物研发全流程智能体初创公司的战略收购。收购完成后，目标团队所拥有的药物筛选与试验智能体算法将被直接集成到买方现有的生命科学专业工具套件中，旨在通过自动化专业Agent加速新药靶点发现与临床流程开发，拓宽其在生物科技高附加值赛道的产业护城河。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio, a startup building specialized AI agents that streamline pharmaceutical drug development pipelines. The technology will be folded into OpenAI's proprietary life sciences platform, accelerating its strategic push into computational biology and automated scientific discovery.

elements_zh.why: 拓展大模型在高壁垒医疗与生物制药产业的深度商业化落地

elements_en.why: Expand enterprise footprint and deep monetization within the lucrative pharmaceutical sector

ai_analysis.insight_en: Charging consumers twenty bucks a month for chatbot banter barely pays the electricity bills, but shortening drug development cycles extracts serious enterprise cash. When the boundless promise of AGI faces quarterly ROI scrutiny, buying your way into the pharmaceutical industry's deep pockets is as pragmatic as it gets.

news.title_zh: 超六千对话泄露致社交巨头急停助手分享
news.summary_zh: 因安全机构发现数千条私密对话链接暴露在公开网络，相关社交平台紧急下线智能助手的网页分享功能

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 知名社交巨头紧急叫停了旗下智能助手的对话在线分享功能。此前第三方网络安全研究机构通过公共域名系统检索追踪，发现超过6800条原本属于用户私人的对话记录链接直接暴露在公网可供外部随意访问。为防止数据泄露风险持续蔓延并配合安全审查，该功能已被临时全面下线。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Meta has suspended the sharing feature on its Muse AI assistant after cybersecurity researchers discovered over 6,800 conversation URLs publicly indexed through open DNS records. The company halted the functionality to investigate security configurations and rethink public link visibility.

elements_zh.why: 功能设计存在公网索引与权限校验疏漏，导致敏感交互数据外泄

elements_en.where: Public DNS records and web-facing assistant endpoints
elements_en.what: Over 6,800 conversation URLs exposed publicly, triggering immediate suspension of sharing
elements_en.why: Insecure link generation and discovery vulnerabilities left user chat logs searchable online

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 社交平台做 AI 助手最擅长的不是技术突破，而是骨子里把用户隐私“昭告天下”的肌肉记忆。几千个本以为是一对一私聊的聊天记录，转头就被公开 DNS 扒个底朝天；这波操作再次生动诠释了什么叫“只要平台不尴尬，尴尬的就是把秘密全吐给大模型的用户”。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Old social networking habits die hard: even when building AI assistants, Meta can't seem to resist turning private user interactions into publicly viewable links. Thousands of private confessions are now forever indexed on public DNS—a masterclass in why you shouldn't tell an AI anything you wouldn't billboard on the highway.

news.title: Foursquare co-founder says the company was acquired a month ago in a deal resulting in a $0 payout for equity holders, and faults leadership installed in 2021 (Dennis Crowley/Teendrama Snippets)

news.original_content:
Dennis Crowley / Teendrama Snippets:
Foursquare co-founder says the company was acquired a month ago in a deal resulting in a $0 payout for equity holders, and faults leadership installed in 2021  —  After 17 years, FSQ's ending has been written.  Some though
news.content_snippet: After 17 years, FSQ's ending has been written. Some thoughts on our final years, an effort to honor the team …
news.summary_en: Foursquare co-founder Dennis Crowley revealed that the 17-year-old location pioneer was quietly acquired a month ago under terms that wiped out common equity holders with a $0 payout. Crowley openly blamed the outcome on mismanagement and flawed strategic pivots orchestrated by leadership appointed in 2021.
news.title_zh: 签到鼻祖卖身出局普通股权益归零
news.summary_zh: 地理位置社交鼻祖在运营十七年后完成被动收购，普通股股东回报清零引发联合创始人痛批管理层

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 移动互联网早期的知名地理签到应用联合创始人公开发文证实，这家成立17年的开拓性企业已在一个月前悄然完成收购退场，但残酷的交易条款导致普通股股东与早期持股员工最终颗粒无收（获得零美元收益）。创始人直接将这一毁灭性结局归咎于公司后期引入的管理团队推行的激进转型策略。

It's a stark reminder of venture capital's brutal mechanics: liquidation preferences save the funds, executives move on, and early employees' equity vanishes into thin air.

news.author: The Information
news.original_content:
The Information:
Sources: Sam Altman told OpenAI staff of three AI endgames: an IAEA-style regulator, a CERN-like lab merger, or one lab using RSI to “melt everyone else's GPUs”  —  OpenAI CEO Sam Altman last week told employees about three proposals t
news.content_snippet: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman last week told employees about three proposals the industry has discussed for how to safely develop AI …
news.summary_en: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman laid out three distinct scenarios for the AI endgame to his staff: establishing an IAEA-style global regulatory watchdog, a multinational lab consolidation modeled after CERN, or a single entity unlocking recursive self-improvement that effectively 'melts everyone else's GPUs' in absolute dominance.
news.title_zh: 奥特曼曝超级智能三大终局剧本
news.summary_zh: 奥特曼向员工描述超级智能的三大可能终局，包括全球强力监管、大国实验室合并或算力彻底赢者通吃

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 在内部面向全员的闭门沟通中，山姆·奥特曼系统阐述了关于通用人工智能未来的三种终极结局：一是效仿国际原子能机构建立强力全球监管实体；二是各大巨头被迫联合组建类似欧洲核子研究中心的全球超级实验室；三是某一家顶尖实验室率先跑通递归自我改进算法，以绝对算力优势直接在物理上“融化掉所有对手的芯片”，形成无可匹敌的绝对单极垄断。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman laid out three distinct scenarios for the AI endgame to his staff: establishing an IAEA-style global regulatory watchdog, a multinational lab consolidation modeled after CERN, or a single entity unlocking recursive self-improvement that effectively 'melts everyone else's GPUs' in absolute dominance.

elements_zh.who: OpenAI首席执行官山姆·奥特曼及内部员工
elements_zh.where: 企业内部全员战略沟通会
elements_zh.what: 提出国际原子能式监管、超大实验室联合或算力绝对碾压的三种AGI终局
elements_zh.why: 向团队强化外部严酷的算力零和博弈现实，为持续激进扩张构筑思想认同

elements_en.what: Outlined three endgame scenarios: IAEA regulator, CERN-style lab merger, or compute monopoly
elements_en.why: Rally internal urgency and justify relentless compute expansion under a zero-sum paradigm

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 奥特曼不愧是全硅谷最擅长讲科幻鬼故事的布道大师，能把赤裸裸的行业洗牌包装成“融化竞争对手的算力芯片”。前两个兼济天下的监管与合作愿景纯属给监管机构看的公关门面，第三个“老子赢者通吃碾碎全场”才是他半夜做梦都在想的真实剧本——毕竟在算力霸权的牌桌上，谁买得起电，谁才能烧光别人的退路。
