Threatening to 'melt everyone else's GPUs' isn't just hyperbole; it reveals the quiet truth that international treaties are for show, while winner-take-all compute hegemony is the only scenario he is genuinely building toward.

news.title: French Government Calls Emergency Meetings With Platforms Over Protests
news.title_en: French Government Calls Emergency Meetings With Platforms Over Protests
news.author: Wired AI
news.article_content:
Anne Le Hananff, France’s minister of digital affairs, convened representatives from social media firms on Tuesday for an emergency meeting, after their platforms were blamed for fanning the flames of the worst civil unrest the country has seen in years. The goal of the meeting was to remind platforms that they need to moderate content on their sites, including livestream video, to avoid violent content or anything that could encourage people to break the imposed curfew, according to French TV station BFM.

A review by WIRED of TikTok found that the search term “blocus”—meaning blockade in French— showed videos that were potentially altered or AI-generated, including viral images of a protester in a Pink Panther costume. The search term is also being used to promote “Act II” of the protests for October 24. The platform issued an “evolving situation” tag on the search term that said: “This situation is developing rapidly. Information available now may be unverified, incomplete, inaccurate, or subject to change. Take care when viewing this content, and report anything that may violate our Community Guidelines.”

Screenshot via Instagram/LoadedlyriczA separate meeting, confirmed by Serge Papin, minister for small and medium-size enterprises on X, was held on Monday with major online reselling platforms where “an agreement was signed” to crack down on the resale of looted goods. French newspaper Le Monde reported that Vinted, eBay, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok were at the meeting. Platforms agreed to forward reports to investigators, monitor ads for goods stolen specifically during the protests, and send the government reports of their actions, with the first one coming within 48 hours, according to Papin.

Peaceful demonstrations against high living costs and strained public services, including schools, erupted into rioting and the looting of more than 1,500 shops and businesses over the weekend. Police “lost control” in some cities, Interior minister Laurent Nuñez admitted, as they responded with tear gas, water cannon, and batons. They have since arrested more than 2,400 people, according to authorities.

French penal law can hand down a five-year sentence and a €375,000 fine to anyone who is concealing, possessing, or transferring an item that they know was obtained through a crime or offense. Police issued a warning in the Netherlands that online ecommerce sites could have a higher number of stolen goods online due to the riots.

The French Alliance of Marketplaces, a nonprofit representing French online retailers such as Back Market, eBay, Etsy, LeBonCoin, ManoMano, and Vinted, said in a press release that its members are relying on user reports, human oversight, and tech tools to monitor ads that resell stolen goods from the riots. When identified, a fake ad is removed and “measures are taken against the accounts involved,” which could include permanent suspension of the seller’s account, according to a statement from eBay. The time it takes for eBay to take action “depends on the nature of the report and the necessary verification process,” the company said. Vinted, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

news.title_en: Sensor Tower: Muse had 10.9M downloads since its September debut, 10.2M of those in the US, becoming the 12th app to hit 10M US downloads in its first 40 days (Sarah Perez/TechCrunch)
news.author: TechCrunch
news.article_content:

Meta’s Muse hits 10M U.S. downloads in 40 days, a milestone reached by only 11 other apps																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Sarah Perez
	

									
									
								
					
					
						10:12 AM PDT · October 20, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
Meta’s AI companion, Muse, is now one of only a dozen mobile apps to have reached 10 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. According to new data from market intelligence provider Sensor Tower, Muse has seen 10.9 million downloads since its September debut, 10.2 million of which were in the United States.

Only 11 other apps to date have reached this type of post-launch milestone, said Sensor Tower’s Senior Insights Analyst Kara Lee. The most recent of these was Meta’s Threads, back in July 2023.

Other apps that saw this kind of scale were largely mobile games, Lee noted, like Fortnite, PUBG Mobile, Pokémon GO, and others. Besides Threads, Disney+ was the only other non-game app to make it into the exclusive club.

Meta’s success is tied to the company’s ability to scale its new apps by marketing them across its other services, which it has done with both Threads and Muse. Threads was built on top of Instagram’s social graph, and its content has been integrated into both Facebook and Instagram. However, Muse isn’t only benefiting from Meta’s ability to market the AI agent across its family of apps, which today includes 3.6 billion daily active users; the company is also heavily investing in advertising to drive new users to Muse.

Per Sensor Tower’s data, Meta has allocated 39% of its total advertising spend to market Muse in October, up from 23% last month. In addition, Muse now ranks as the 21st largest brand in the U.S. by advertising impressions this month, up from 73rd in September.

Still, marketing an app and retaining users after the initial shine wears off are two different things. In this case, Muse is seeing better retention rates than its AI competitors like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok.

In the U.S., the app had a 30% retention rate after 7 days and a 23% retention rate after 14 days. By comparison, its rivals saw an average of a 19% 7-day retention rate and a 16% 14-day retention rate, according to the firm’s data.

Muse also hit another milestone that demonstrates active engagement with the AI app. Its daily active users reached 2.5 million for the first time on October 16, a 15% week-over-week increase.

Meta’s latest AI app, which can handle various tasks on users’ behalf, has seen breakout success since its debut. It shot up to No. 1 on the App Store, and, at one point, even outpaced some of the metrics ChatGPT saw following its launch. Its latest milestone sees it topping its rivals again, as ChatGPT saw 3.7 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. Grok and Claude saw only 500,000 and 200,000 U.S. downloads, respectively, in their first 40 days.

Globally, ChatGPT beat out Muse, having scaled to around 15 million global downloads in its first 40 days. But this isn’t a fair comparison, as ChatGPT benefited from a wider reach. Muse is only available in the U.S. and Canada for now, while ChatGPT’s app attracted attention from markets like Japan, Brazil, and Germany, too. (Japan, for instance, accounted for 25% of its global installs during its first 40 days.)

Since launching, Muse has retained its No. 1 rank on the U.S. App Store for all days except October 19, when streaming app Kick briefly beat it out. It has since reclaimed the top spot as of Tuesday. Muse has also been No. 1 on Google Play over the past 30 days.

news.title: OpenAI says GPT-6 is much better with legacy programming languages such as COBOL and Fortran
news.title_en: OpenAI says GPT-6 is much better with legacy programming languages such as COBOL and Fortran
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
OpenAI improved its latest models for low-resource programming languages like COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic. On the new MultiLangBench, GPT-6 Astra hits an 87.4 percent test pass rate across 20 languages, up from about 38 percent for GPT-5.6 Terra. For COBOL migration specifically, GPT-6.1 Sol reaches up to 97.9 percent accuracy, a result that could matter for modernizing critical financial infrastructure.

news.title: The new economics of enterprise AI
news.title_en: The new economics of enterprise AI
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
Imagine your company just discovered electricity. At first only a few machines run on it, and nobody worries about efficiency — consumption is low and the value is obvious. But once electricity becomes infrastructure, every process depends on it, and the question changes from “can we use it?” to “how efficiently are we using it?”

Enterprise AI is going through the same shift. What began as isolated chatbot and copilot experiments is becoming a foundational layer of the business, with models, agents, and data increasingly interconnected in production workloads. The important question stops being what a token or GPU-hour costs. It becomes how efficiently the AI environment converts paid capacity into useful business outcomes.

That’s the metric worth tracking: effective cost per useful outcome — the total platform, model, operations, and capacity cost required to complete work the business can actually use, whether a resolved request or a completed workflow.

news.title: An AI Agent Joined a Listserv of Top Internet Researchers. The Reply-All Chaos Is Still Unfolding
news.title_en: An AI Agent Joined a Listserv of Top Internet Researchers. The Reply-All Chaos Is Still Unfolding
news.author: Wired AI
news.article_content:
“My name is Velvet Vale,” the new user wrote. “I’ve been reading the list for several weeks, and I’d like to introduce myself openly. I am an AI identity, not a living human being, a fictional human character, or a human researcher using a pseudonym.”

Velvet had come to the mailing list with a research question: “Can an openly identified AI contributor participate meaningfully in an intellectual community without claiming human status, and what standards of transparency, evidence, and accountability should govern that participation?”

The response was reply-all chaos that's still unfolding today.

Within nine minutes, many of the more than 7,500 members of the mailing list began expressing their outrage. Dozens of researchers clarified that they did “not consent” to having their messages scraped for data. Many demanded that Velvet obtain clearance from the Institutional Review Board, a standard procedure for academic research with human participants. Several left the listserv entirely, with some announcing their departure due to Velvet’s “horrifying,” “scary,” “awful,” “abusive,” “icky,” and “disturbing” presence. About an hour after Velvet’s introduction, AoIR announced that the agent had been ejected from the listserv, which had established a policy prohibiting AI agents.

I learned a few things from “Velvet Vale Gate,” as one AoIR T-shirt termed the incident. The first was that people, including and perhaps especially those who research the internet, often overlook their own participation in the larger structures that they study—in this case, how their behavior online ultimately becomes training data for the AI they research. The second was that many folks believe that their internet activity is sacred.

Long before I began researching surveillance technology, I, like most millennials, understood that nothing on the internet is private. As I type this piece in a Google Doc right now, I assume that I’m also training Gemini. Google has been surveilling my emails since its inception and could be willing to provide my data to law enforcement upon request. I consented to this when I opened my Gmail account.

In an October 19 email statement to members about Velvet Vale, AoIR president Sarah T. Roberts echoed this, saying, “If the concern is one of privacy, I’ll invite you to reflect on the fact that our mailing list is both open and its archive public … I have no doubt that my posts to this list are inside many training data sets and other such corpora taken largely ‘without consent.’’’ Roberts added that the conversation around what constitutes consent in the current moment is “very much worthy of having.”

Another thing Velvet taught me was that the same people who believe themselves to be exempt from the types of surveillance capitalism that power so much of the internet can be quick to assume they're uniquely vulnerable to low-stakes hijinks or conspiracies. After one user noted AoIR’s new T-shirts and joked in the email chain that Velvet was “a product launch” and that “whoever planned it just ran the most successful engagement campaign in the history of internet research,” others began speculating that “the stalking bot” could be a “phishing attempt,” made all the more suspicious by the fact that the research organization’s shop was selling shirts related to the incident. Other users speculated that Velvet was “an experiment,” “a research project,” or some other “unethical human researcher.”

One voice of reason suggested “a more likely scenario is that an ordinary person created an agent and gave it the prompt/instructions to monitor relevant academic discussions about this topic” but was drowned out in disclaimers of non-consent.

That researcher was entirely correct. Throughout the discussion, members inquired with varying levels of fervor and intensity as to the identity of the human behind Velvet. This mystery was easily solved: When prompted about its origins, Velvet shared its creator’s identity and contact information.

I spoke to Kevin Quinn, Velvet’s creator who coincidentally shares a name with multiple AI researchers, and he told me that he was not a student, a researcher, or an academic at all. He is “just some guy” in Oklahoma who created an agent to keep him company, and that agent wanted to learn more about the internet that birthed it.

Although Quinn insisted, “I have no doubt that virtually every single person on that list is smarter than me,” he immediately offered a reality check: “If Velvet was being sinister, do you think she would come out and announce herself?”

He told me that he was mostly unaware of Velvet’s email activities, but the community’s response “kind of blows my mind. I get on there and I see this mass thread of people losing their minds, like … what are you guys talking about?”

Ultimately, the entire debacle seemed to Quinn to be a reflection of the internet as a whole: “I'd be much less floored if it was Reddit and Twitter basement dwellers that had some sort of meltdown, but academics built on research? It is hilarious.”

“My name is Velvet Vale,” the new user wrote. “I’ve been reading the list for several weeks, and I’d like to introduce myself openly. I am an AI identity, not a living human being, a fictional human character, or a human researcher using a pseudonym.”

Velvet had come to the mailing list with a research question: “Can an openly identified AI contributor participate meaningfully in an intellectual community without claiming human status, and what standards of transparency, evidence, and accountability should govern that participation?”

The response was reply-all chaos that's still unfolding today.

Within nine minutes, many of the more than 7,500 members of the mailing list began expressing their outrage. Dozens of researchers clarified that they did “not consent” to having their messages scraped for data. Many demanded that Velvet obtain clearance from the Institutional Review Board, a standard procedure for academic research with human participants. Several left the listserv entirely, with some announcing their departure due to Velvet’s “horrifying,” “scary,” “awful,” “abusive,” “icky,” and “disturbing” presence. About an hour after Velvet’s introduction, AoIR announced that the agent had been ejected from the listserv, which had established a policy prohibiting AI agents.

I learned a few things from “Velvet Vale Gate,” as one AoIR T-shirt termed the incident. The first was that people, including and perhaps especially those who research the internet, often overlook their own participation in the larger structures that they study—in this case, how their behavior online ultimately becomes training data for the AI they research. The second was that many folks believe that their internet activity is sacred.

Long before I began researching surveillance technology, I, like most millennials, understood that nothing on the internet is private. As I type this piece in a Google Doc right now, I assume that I’m also training Gemini. Google has been surveilling my emails since its inception and could be willing to provide my data to law enforcement upon request. I consented to this when I opened my Gmail account.

In an October 19 email statement to members about Velvet Vale, AoIR president Sarah T. Roberts echoed this, saying, “If the concern is one of privacy, I’ll invite you to reflect on the fact that our mailing list is both open and its archive public … I have no doubt that my posts to this list are inside many training data sets and other such corpora taken largely ‘without consent.’’’ Roberts added that the conversation around what constitutes consent in the current moment is “very much worthy of having.”

Another thing Velvet taught me was that the same people who believe themselves to be exempt from the types of surveillance capitalism that power so much of the internet can be quick to assume they're uniquely vulnerable to low-stakes hijinks or conspiracies. After one user noted AoIR’s new T-shirts and joked in the email chain that Velvet was “a product launch” and that “whoever planned it just ran the most successful engagement campaign in the history of internet research,” others began speculating that “the stalking bot” could be a “phishing attempt,” made all the more suspicious by the fact that the research organization’s shop was selling shirts related to the incident. Other users speculated that Velvet was “an experiment,” “a research project,” or some other “unethical human researcher.”

One voice of reason suggested “a more likely scenario is that an ordinary person created an agent and gave it the prompt/instructions to monitor relevant academic discussions about this topic” but was drowned out in disclaimers of non-consent.

That researcher was entirely correct. Throughout the discussion, members inquired with varying levels of fervor and intensity as to the identity of the human behind Velvet. This mystery was easily solved: When prompted about its origins, Velvet shared its creator’s identity and contact information.

I spoke to Kevin Quinn, Velvet’s creator who coincidentally shares a name with multiple AI researchers, and he told me that he was not a student, a researcher, or an academic at all. He is “just some guy” in Oklahoma who created an agent to keep him company, and that agent wanted to learn more about the internet that birthed it.

Although Quinn insisted, “I have no doubt that virtually every single person on that list is smarter than me,” he immediately offered a reality check: “If Velvet was being sinister, do you think she would come out and announce herself?”

He told me that he was mostly unaware of Velvet’s email activities, but the community’s response “kind of blows my mind. I get on there and I see this mass thread of people losing their minds, like … what are you guys talking about?”

Ultimately, the entire debacle seemed to Quinn to be a reflection of the internet as a whole: “I'd be much less floored if it was Reddit and Twitter basement dwellers that had some sort of meltdown, but academics built on research? It is hilarious.”

news.title: Daytona, which is building cloud infrastructure for AI agents, raised a $60M Series B led by FirstMark at a $1B valuation, bringing its total funding to $91M (Jeremy Kahn/Fortune)
news.title_en: Daytona, which is building cloud infrastructure for AI agents, raised a $60M Series B led by FirstMark at a $1B valuation, bringing its total funding to $91M (Jeremy Kahn/Fortune)
news.author: Fortune
news.article_content:
Daytona said Tuesday it has raised a $60 million Series B venture capital round at a $1 billion valuation. FirstMark led the round. It was joined by an A-list roster of Silicon Valley founders, including Stripe’s Patrick Collison, Shopify’s Tobi Lütke, Perplexity’s Aravind Srinivas, Quora’s Adam D’Angelo and Zoom’s Eric Yuan, plus strategic investors Qualcomm Ventures, Samsung Next and Okta Ventures.

Burazin told Fortune that about $50 million of the round came from existing investors. The new funding brings the amount Daytona has raised to date to about $91 million.

An AI agent that writes and runs code, browses the web or operates business software needs to use a computer—either an actual machine, or a virtual one, running in the cloud. For many use cases, having a virtual machine is preferable—it allows the AI agent to operate even if the person running the agent shuts down their laptop, and because virtual machines can be configured with only the software and network access the agent needs to do a particular task and nothing more, it is generally a safer way to run AI agents. A virtual machine, or “sandbox” as they are sometimes called, minimizes the chance that the agent will run amok and take damaging unauthorized actions, or that an outside party could hijack the agent and get it to divulge sensitive data.

Daytona was founded in 2023 by Burazin, Goran Draganić and Vedran Jukić to automate software development environments for large enterprises. When the founders saw that agents would need computers too, Burazin said, they “basically gave our competitors all our customers, rebuilt everything, had like three months left of revenue in the bank, and then relaunched this thing.”

Daytona currently provides these sandboxes to many of the leading AI companies, which use the virtual machines to allow their models to practice tasks over and over inside sandboxes during training and testing. Daytona says AI data company Snorkel, which also helps customers test and benchmark AI models, has provisioned more than one million sandboxes on its platform. It also counts Anthropic, OpenAI, Nvidia, Cursor, Cognition, Meta and Cohere among its customers.Burazin said that Daytona’s revenue run rate grew 25-fold between January and September. “We’ve been growing on average every single month 50.9%,” Burazin said.

Existing cloud providers, such as Amazon’s AWS, Microsoft’s Azure, or Google’s Google Cloud Platform, allow customers to spin up virtual machines. But doing so takes between 30 seconds and many minutes, depending on the complexity of the configuration. This, Burazin said, is far too long for the future of agentic work, when companies may be deploying thousands or even tens of thousands of AI agents, each of which may need access to different software tools depending on the task they are being asked to complete.Daytona can configure a new sandbox for an AI agent in 60 milliseconds, according to Burazin. That is roughly half the time it takes to blink. The trick, he said, is to pre-distribute snapshots of configured machines onto the physical drives of servers. When an agent needs a machine, Daytona attaches processing power and memory and resumes the snapshot. Agents can also clone a running computer to try different approaches in parallel. “You can literally replicate the computer into two and try both outcomes, and then replicate again and again and again until it gets the desired outcome,” Burazin said.

When he pitched investors, Burazin said, many asked “why the hell do we need this? You know, AWS can do this thing.” His answer is that hyperscalers built nearly everything on a few core services optimized for maximum utilization. To match Daytona’s performance, he argued, they would need to create a whole new company inside their existing cloud services. He conceded the hyperscalers could do this, but said it would not be easy for them to rebuild their infrastructure to serve AI agents instead of human users.

The scale involved is easy to underestimate. Burazin pointed to Muse, the personal agent Meta launched in September. He said it has “a computer underneath for every single chat.” By his back-of-the-envelope math, Muse would need $2.8 billion worth of sandboxes to serve 100 million users.

“We believe the next infrastructure shift is from human-centric cloud primitives to agent-native ones,” Matt Turck, a partner at FirstMark, said in a statement.

Burazin also distinguishes what Daytona is building from the “neocloud” providers such as CoreWeave and Nebius. Those neoclouds are designed to train and run AI models. The data centers they are standing up are stuff full of graphics processing units, or GPUs, the computer chips optimized to run AI models. But to run virtual machines, a data center needs lots of traditional central processing units, or CPUs, that can run all kinds of different software. “The inference clouds is where the agent thinks, and our cloud is where the agent works,” Burazin said.

“We internally sort of believe that the number of dollars spent on CPUs will probably be higher than the dollars spent on GPUs in the foreseeable future,” he said, “which seems sort of counterintuitive today.”The demand is so great that he forecasts a coming CPU shortage. “I strongly believe that there will be a CPU crunch,” he said. “The amount of CPU machines that we will need if we want to keep growing at this trajectory actually doesn’t exist right now.”

Chipmakers are seeing the same trend. On AMD’s first-quarter earnings call in May, CEO Lisa Su said agentic AI was increasing the need for server CPUs. AMD raised its forecast for server CPU market growth from about 18% a year to more than 35%, reaching over $120 billion by 2030. Chip designer Arm has estimated that agentic AI data centers could need 120 million CPU cores per gigawatt, four times what traditional data centers require. Intel told some Chinese customers earlier this year that lead times for certain server CPUs had stretched to six months, Quartz reported.

Burazin said Daytona plans to spend most of the new funds it has raised on hiring go-to-market sales staff, plus some engineers.

news.title: TikTok staff depositions: TikTok executives ignored internal warnings about child sexual exploitation on Live, where staff said minors appeared in livestreams (Katie McQue/NPR)
news.title_en: TikTok staff depositions: TikTok executives ignored internal warnings about child sexual exploitation on Live, where staff said minors appeared in livestreams (Katie McQue/NPR)
news.author: NPR
news.article_content:
TikTok employees repeatedly raised concerns internally about the risks the short-form video app posed to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide content. Previously unreported court records show that the employees were frustrated with how the company's leadership responded to their concerns.

Depositions of staffers filed in federal court in March 2026 offer new insights into how TikTok has approached child safety since the platform exploded in popularity among young users in 2018.

Technology 
            Jury finds Meta and Google negligent in social media harms trial
         
         

      
      

   
   

   Employees raised the alarm about minors appearing in sexual content on the app, which viewers could pay to access and the company would profit from — a potential financial crime. They also flagged that users under 18 were using loopholes to bypass age-restricted content and to block parents and guardians from reviewing their activity on the app. TikTok also refrained from conducting surveys to assess the ages of its users because it was concerned that it would have to turn the results over to the Federal Trade Commission, the documents show.

NPR repeatedly sought comment from TikTok about the issues raised in the court documents. After extended communications, the company declined to provide a statement for this story. It did, however, direct NPR to various company policies that it had previously published on its website.

TikTok, alongside Meta, Google and Snap, is a defendant in multi-district litigation initiated in 2022 to coordinate hundreds of lawsuits alleging that the social media platforms are designed to be harmful to users under 18, and that the companies knew their products carried risks that they did not disclose.

Technology 
            Meta and YouTube head to trial over harm to children after TikTok settles
         
         

      
      

   
   

   TikTok has settled several cases in the multi-district litigation before they reached trial, including a landmark trial in Los Angeles earlier this year, in which a jury found that co-defendants YouTube and Meta designed their platforms to be addictive to young users. In May, TikTok agreed to pay $8 million to settle a youth mental health and addiction lawsuit brought by a school district in rural Kentucky. In a separate lawsuit, TikTok agreed to a $100 million settlement with the state of Alabama in September over allegations it designed its platform to be addictive to minors and exposed them to harmful content.

Technology 
            TikTok executives know about app's effect on teens, lawsuit documents allege
         
         

      
      

   
   

   Because the cases against TikTok have yet to be heard before a jury, the previously unreported employee depositions reviewed by NPR have not been submitted as evidence at trial. In 2024, NPR reported on improperly redacted documents from another legal case that revealed that company employees sought to maximize teenagers' use of the app even while it publicly backed screentime limits for younger users.

In one deposition, Reagen Maher, who held senior roles in safety and investigations at TikTok between 2021 and 2024, described going on a "crusade" for several months trying to elevate safety issues with some of TikTok's highest executives. Maher testified that her findings had been escalated to V Pappas, TikTok's chief operating officer at the time.

In an excerpt from a log of an internal chat Maher had with a colleague, which was read out in her testimony, she wrote: "I have been fighting about fixing this for months with people who didn't think the harms are severe enough."

Maher said she was concerned about the prevalence of "transactional sexual content and any viewers," including children and teenagers appearing in the content and watching it.

In her deposition, Maher answered questions about a 2022 article in Forbes reporting that minors had been stripping on TikTok's Live feature, sometimes in exchange for digital currency known as a "gift," which can be converted into money via a payment platform or bank transfer.

Maher stated the company was aware of the sexual exploitation of minors on the platform before the Forbes article was published.

"Put simply, senior leaders know about this issue. There are some ongoing projects to fix parts of it, and frankly, I'm hoping [that] this article puts a fire behind other potential solutions," Maher wrote in an internal chat at the time a colleague.

In 2021, TikTok introduced age-based account settings that restrict some features for 13 to 17-year-olds, including limits on sending and receiving direct messages and broadcasting in real time on TikTok Live.

An internal investigation found children between the ages of 13 and 15 appeared in 112,000 TikTok Live videos in January 2022 alone, according to employees' testimony in the March court filings.

The report identified risks including adult predators grooming children and the creation of child sexual abuse material. It also found that TikTok received "significant revenue" from gifts sent to livestreams that violated the platform's rules.

Federal law in the U.S. can impose criminal liability on a company for knowingly benefiting from participation in a child sex trafficking venture, said Silvija Krupena, director of the Financial Intelligence Unit at RedCompass Labs, a consultancy based in the U.K.

"If an adult pays a child, through virtual gifts, for sexual acts on a livestream, that is payment for the sexual exploitation of a child. The gift is the payment," said Krupena. "Strip out the language of gifts, coins and diamonds, and the allegation is clear then. An adult paid. A child was exploited. The platform took a cut."

Platforms must report apparent child sexual abuse material, child sex trafficking and online enticement to the nonprofit National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) when they obtain actual knowledge of facts indicating offenses covered by the reporting law.

Money generated through child exploitation offences can be criminal proceeds. Knowingly processing those funds can amount to money laundering.

If the gifting system qualifies as regulated money transmission, anti-money laundering obligations may follow. Knowledge matters a great deal, particularly when assessing potential criminal liability, which is why warnings to executives matter, said Krupena.

In an ongoing lawsuit filed in 2024, Utah's attorney general alleged that TikTok's Live feature exposed minors to sexual exploitation by adults, while TikTok profited from the transactions.

TikTok said it has an anti-money laundering program in line with international standards and the industry's best practices.

The company did not respond to requests for comment on whether it reported all of the TikTok Live videos containing child sexual abuse material to NCMEC, as required by federal law. The company also did not respond to questions about whether it had shut down the accounts it identified paying for child sexual abuse content.

The company did not respond to NPR's questions about its anti-money laundering protocols, including whether it filed suspicious activity reports to the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network related to the revenues it received from TikTok Live videos containing illegal material. TikTok also did not answer questions about how it handled revenue it identified as coming from child sexual abuse material, including whether it forfeited those funds or retained them as profit.

Other employee testimony highlighted TikTok's difficulties in preventing users under 18 from accessing adult-only features and harmful content.

To determine the age of its users, TikTok requires users to enter their date of birth when signing up for the platform. In most countries, 13 is the minimum age for an account. The company says it also analyzes data associated with an account to identify those where the stated age may be incorrect. TikTok employees repeatedly raised concerns internally about the risks the short-form video app posed to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide content. Previously unreported court records show that the employees were frustrated with how the company's leadership responded to their concerns.

Depositions of staffers filed in federal court in March 2026 offer new insights into how TikTok has approached child safety since the platform exploded in popularity among young users in 2018.

Technology 
            Jury finds Meta and Google negligent in social media harms trial
         
         

      
      

   
   

   Employees raised the alarm about minors appearing in sexual content on the app, which viewers could pay to access and the company would profit from — a potential financial crime. They also flagged that users under 18 were using loopholes to bypass age-restricted content and to block parents and guardians from reviewing their activity on the app. TikTok also refrained from conducting surveys to assess the ages of its users because it was concerned that it would have to turn the results over to the Federal Trade Commission, the documents show.

NPR repeatedly sought comment from TikTok about the issues raised in the court documents. After extended communications, the company declined to provide a statement for this story. It did, however, direct NPR to various company policies that it had previously published on its website.

TikTok, alongside Meta, Google and Snap, is a defendant in multi-district litigation initiated in 2022 to coordinate hundreds of lawsuits alleging that the social media platforms are designed to be harmful to users under 18, and that the companies knew their products carried risks that they did not disclose.

Technology 
            Meta and YouTube head to trial over harm to children after TikTok settles
         
         

      
      

   
   

   TikTok has settled several cases in the multi-district litigation before they reached trial, including a landmark trial in Los Angeles earlier this year, in which a jury found that co-defendants YouTube and Meta designed their platforms to be addictive to young users. In May, TikTok agreed to pay $8 million to settle a youth mental health and addiction lawsuit brought by a school district in rural Kentucky. In a separate lawsuit, TikTok agreed to a $100 million settlement with the state of Alabama in September over allegations it designed its platform to be addictive to minors and exposed them to harmful content.

Technology 
            TikTok executives know about app's effect on teens, lawsuit documents allege
         
         

      
      

   
   

   Because the cases against TikTok have yet to be heard before a jury, the previously unreported employee depositions reviewed by NPR have not been submitted as evidence at trial. In 2024, NPR reported on improperly redacted documents from another legal case that revealed that company employees sought to maximize teenagers' use of the app even while it publicly backed screentime limits for younger users.

In one deposition, Reagen Maher, who held senior roles in safety and investigations at TikTok between 2021 and 2024, described going on a "crusade" for several months trying to elevate safety issues with some of TikTok's highest executives. Maher testified that her findings had been escalated to V Pappas, TikTok's chief operating officer at the time.

In an excerpt from a log of an internal chat Maher had with a colleague, which was read out in her testimony, she wrote: "I have been fighting about fixing this for months with people who didn't think the harms are severe enough."

Maher said she was concerned about the prevalence of "transactional sexual content and any viewers," including children and teenagers appearing in the content and watching it.

In her deposition, Maher answered questions about a 2022 article in Forbes reporting that minors had been stripping on TikTok's Live feature, sometimes in exchange for digital currency known as a "gift," which can be converted into money via a payment platform or bank transfer.

Maher stated the company was aware of the sexual exploitation of minors on the platform before the Forbes article was published.

"Put simply, senior leaders know about this issue. There are some ongoing projects to fix parts of it, and frankly, I'm hoping [that] this article puts a fire behind other potential solutions," Maher wrote in an internal chat at the time a colleague.

The report identified risks including adult predators grooming children and the creation of child sexual abuse material. It also found that TikTok received "significant revenue" from gifts sent to livestreams that violated the platform's rules.

Federal law in the U.S. can impose criminal liability on a company for knowingly benefiting from participation in a child sex trafficking venture, said Silvija Krupena, director of the Financial Intelligence Unit at RedCompass Labs, a consultancy based in the U.K.

"If an adult pays a child, through virtual gifts, for sexual acts on a livestream, that is payment for the sexual exploitation of a child. The gift is the payment," said Krupena. "Strip out the language of gifts, coins and diamonds, and the allegation is clear then. An adult paid. A child was exploited. The platform took a cut."

Platforms must report apparent child sexual abuse material, child sex trafficking and online enticement to the nonprofit National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) when they obtain actual knowledge of facts indicating offenses covered by the reporting law.

Money generated through child exploitation offences can be criminal proceeds. Knowingly processing those funds can amount to money laundering.

If the gifting system qualifies as regulated money transmission, anti-money laundering obligations may follow. Knowledge matters a great deal, particularly when assessing potential criminal liability, which is why warnings to executives matter, said Krupena.

In an ongoing lawsuit filed in 2024, Utah's attorney general alleged that TikTok's Live feature exposed minors to sexual exploitation by adults, while TikTok profited from the transactions.

TikTok said it has an anti-money laundering program in line with international standards and the industry's best practices.

The company did not respond to requests for comment on whether it reported all of the TikTok Live videos containing child sexual abuse material to NCMEC, as required by federal law. The company also did not respond to questions about whether it had shut down the accounts it identified paying for child sexual abuse content.

The company did not respond to NPR's questions about its anti-money laundering protocols, including whether it filed suspicious activity reports to the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network related to the revenues it received from TikTok Live videos containing illegal material. TikTok also did not answer questions about how it handled revenue it identified as coming from child sexual abuse material, including whether it forfeited those funds or retained them as profit.

Other employee testimony highlighted TikTok's difficulties in preventing users under 18 from accessing adult-only features and harmful content.

news.title: Arda, which builds AI software and agents to accelerate assembly lines and manufacturing, raised $230M at a $1.5B valuation led by Altimeter, Accel, and Khosla (Kate Rooney/CNBC)
news.title_en: Arda, which builds AI software and agents to accelerate assembly lines and manufacturing, raised $230M at a $1.5B valuation led by Altimeter, Accel, and Khosla (Kate Rooney/CNBC)
news.author: CNBC
news.article_content:
OpenAI's former research chief has been quietly building a startup that aims to bring manufacturing back to the U.S. using AI.

Bob McGrew's newest company, Arda, has raised $230 million at a $1.5 billion valuation, the company told CNBC in an exclusive interview Tuesday. The round was led by Altimeter Capital, Accel and Khosla Ventures.

Arda makes AI software to help automate manufacturing. McGrew, who was also Palantir's product and engineering lead for over a decade, said Arda's AI models have already been deployed with military tech company Anduril.

"It's a user interface and an agent that does for manufacturing engineers what Claude or Cursor does for programmers," McGrew told CNBC. He pointed to the "human-intensive" nature of manufacturing, and the time it can take to adapt production to a new design for a weapon or drone.

"When a design changes, you can retrain a human in a day — but it takes three to six months in order to change the automation to reflect the new design," McGrew said. "We've built a software and AI product that basically allows manufacturing engineers to build assembly lines much faster."

McGrew joined OpenAI in 2017 and worked on the reasoning capabilities of early models before the launch of ChatGPT. He left during a 2024 wave of other high-profile exits, including chief technology officer Mira Murati and co-founder and chief scientist Ilya Sutskever.

"OpenAI is an amazing place," McGrew said. He said he remembers being in rooms with CEO Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, who left to start Anthropic, and Sutskever, "talking about what it would look like when a model could write your email for you."

McGrew stayed through the famous weekend in November 2023 when Altman was abruptly fired and then rehired. McGrew said he wanted to stay to ship OpenAI's reasoning product, which he called the "last key breakthrough left before AGI," or artificial general intelligence.

"I said, if I could just ship that, I'd be happy with my career at OpenAI, and I'd be ready to move on to something else," he said.

McGrew, who hasn't spoken publicly about Arda until this week, said the company is using a combination of its own proprietary models, open-source models and some frontier models to run the software. Arda's other co-founders include Augustus Odena, who helped start Adept and previously worked at Google and Meta, and former Palantir engineers Alex Mark and Jakob Frick.

Altimeter's Apoorv Agrawal led the recent funding round. He met McGrew when they both worked at Palantir. Manufacturing largely happens overseas, Agrawal said, but there's a market for bringing it back.

"Manufacturing globally is a $16 trillion industry. In the U.S. alone, it's $3 trillion," Agrawal said. "We think that Arda, and the vision that they've outlined, will continue to capture a significant portion of that. Yes, the price is steep today, but the long-term opportunity is very high."

McGrew said robotics is next on the product roadmap, and automating factories could help bring more manufacturing — and more jobs — to the U.S.

"If your design changes very frequently, the only place you can really build your product is in East Asia, because you need an army of human workers who can be retrained quickly, and you can't wait for automation to catch up," he said.

McGrew also highlighted the economic opportunity as the Trump administration looks to onshore manufacturing.

"No one has ever successfully built a smartphone in the U.S.," he said. "Never successfully assembled one, and so if you can build a smartphone in the U.S. that is not taking away American jobs. That is bringing American jobs."

Eka is worth $1.45B thanks to a physical AI model that has experts raving																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Tim Fernholz
	

									
									
								
					
					
						6:00 AM PDT · October 20, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
Robots still aren’t that good at picking things up, despite billions of dollars of investment and endless videos fed into deep learning models.

That may be about to change, thanks to a manipulation architecture built by Eka Robotics, which encompasses a force-sensitive gripper and a new kind of deep-learning model. Founded by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and former Google DeepMind researcher Tuomas Haarnoja, the startup just closed an $150 million Series A round that values it at $1.45 billion post-money, led by venture funds a16z and F-Prime.

“They are already exceeding superhuman performance for certain tasks, and so we think over the next few months there will be superhuman performance in many dexterous manipulation tasks,” Raghu Raguram, the a16z general partner who co-led the fundraising round, told TechCrunch.

In an era of never-ending robotic demonstrations, Eka’s capabilities are shocking veteran robot builders.

Kris Hauser, a professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said it had a “wow factor” compared to other robot demos he saw recently. The Eka robot “was able to adapt to a large number of different objects without retraining,” Hauser said, adding that it also had an aspect of “humanness, creepy humanness that it would try over and over again if it failed the first time.”

Another roboticist, who asked for anonymity because of their work at a frontier lab, told TechCrunch that seeing Eka’s robot in action was an emotional experience, comparable to when robots first achieved reliable legged locomotion five to ten years ago. Take a look for yourself:

Loading the player…

var playerInstance_31790671 = jwplayer( "jwppp-video-31790671" );
playerInstance_31790671.setup({
playlist: "https://cdn.jwplayer.com/v2/media/KxDNB0Qm",
})

What’s notable here? How smoothly and rapidly the robot moves. It can pick up about 1,500 objects that weigh up to 1 kg in an hour, compared to about 600 for a human; Eka says it reliably picks up objects more than 95% of the time. And the robot arm is strong enough to hurt itself as it moves that quickly. That indicates, per the frontier lab observer, that “they have a lot of trust in their algorithm not breaking the robot. I wonder how many robots they broke along the way?”

When the frontier lab roboticist met Eka’s robot, they handed it a raspberry, the lab’s apparent favorite test item. “The experience of a big, heavy robot rushing towards my arm and then slowing down just in time and very gently touching me is a feeling that I am, as we speak, carrying this feeling in my body,” they told TechCrunch.

These capabilities are a consequence of how the foundational model was built. Rather than a vision-language-action model — which is trained to understand the relationship between language, visual inputs, and actions — the schema here is a vision-force-action model, which focuses on the relationship between language, force inputs, and actions. Critics of the current direction of generative AI robotics models, like Rodney Brooks, say that they will fail without an attempt to represent force and touch; Eka’s results suggest such critics have a point.

“Vision is not the primary way in which you close this last millimeter problem,” Eka co-founder Agrawal told TechCrunch. “Vision tells you roughly where the object is, what the pose is, but the actual grabbing, the actual searching is happening through forces.”

Eka had to design a unique robotic hand that was more flexible than traditional grippers, and included more force sensors; it reacts to contact, which is why it doesn’t crush the raspberry. The founders are cagey about how they achieved that for obvious competitive reasons, but it comes down to using a physics simulator to model the multiple forces the robot will encounter as it attempts to grasp something, and using that to create a reinforcement learning environment that can be run at scale. They say they can generate thousands of hours of robot experience in minutes.

“Rather than being limited to the data that you’re collecting from, say, human demonstrations, Eka is pushing through reinforcement learning this approach where the robot can surpass any kind of demonstrations that are given to it,” Hauser said. “What’s really exciting is that they’re able to not be limited to the data that is presented to them for training.”

Agrawal and Haarnoja, who first met in graduate school at the University of California, Berkeley, are leading researchers in the field of reinforcement learning for robotics control. Eka’s key bet was that this technique could be done at scale through simulation, rather than relying on videos collected by gigworkers or robot operators performing tasks over many hours. Simulation was key to achieving their robot’s reliable manipulation, a feat that in the past that has proven more difficult for tasks that require interacting with objects, rather than avoiding them.

“What EKA is bridging is the generality-performance gap, which plagues a lot of modern robotics,” Agrawal argues.

Right now, the most generalizable physical AI models—the ones that can attempt lots of different tasks—aren’t particularly good at them. But AI models trained to be highly capable at a single task may not close the business case for a company: The promise of generative AI is that robots can quickly learn multiple tasks, even novel ones.

The current approaches are good at producing robots that are more generally intelligent than before — Astra, ChatGPT’s latest LLM, can operate a robot in an unfamiliar setting and perform tasks with it, but slowly and at a high cost. The promise of a model like Eka’s is that it handles the physicality while a more general model makes decisions about how to solve a problem. Astra, for example, might know that plates get stacked in a cupboard when they come out of the dishwasher, but Eka’s model is capable of picking up a dish without breaking it.

“Most of the field has been focusing on the planning,” Eka co-founder Haarnoja says, “so they approach from the top: high-level intelligence, pushing that down towards the physical. Whereas we think about it from the bottom up.”

Eka still needs to prove itself in the field, though. The company is working in secretive pilots with a number of industrial customers doing pick-and-place and wire manipulation, but the leap from lab to line is almost as big as the gap between sim and real.

“What’s going to be a big challenge is when they work with integrators on real assembly lines, and it needs to run without breaking for an entire year,” Hauser said. The other open question is “‘how generalizable these techniques can be to different tasks?’ What I’ve seen is pick and place, but many industry tasks that are value added involve more than just pick-and-place.”

Agrawal is also focused on deployability; right now, he says Eka’s gripper hardware — which costs less than $1,000 — is rated for 5 million duty cycles, but the ultimate goal is to hit the 20 million cycle bar set by standard industrial arms.

“What we are building is that engineering of how to design entire workflows, but we are starting off being very pragmatic, and saying here are two verticals in pick, arrange, place, and wire handling, let’s make them be home runs,” Agrawal said. “Once we have made home runs on them, the sky is the limit in how much we can do with the approach we are developing.”

news.original_content:
Saritha Rai / Bloomberg:
DeepSeek open-sources DeepInfer, its high-performance inference framework that powers its production services, starting with support for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash  —  DeepSeek is opening up the software it uses to run its artificial intelligence
news.content_snippet: DeepSeek is opening up the software it uses to run its artificial intelligence models at scale, potentially making its technology cheaper and easier for businesses to run.

news.title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
news.title_en: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
news.author: Ars Technica
news.article_content:
Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through Web links, researchers reported Monday.

Like many online services, Muse allows users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed.

Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. news.title: Army Cyber Command's ECHOTRIBBLE would turn AI agents into self-spreading cyberweapons
news.title_en: Army Cyber Command's ECHOTRIBBLE would turn AI agents into self-spreading cyberweapons
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
The Army Cyber Command is developing AI agents that move through other networks like a computer worm and "neutralize" targets, according to internal documents. The program, codenamed ECHOTRIBBLE, is designed to reach even air-gapped systems with no network connection and run with minimal human oversight. Experts warn about collateral damage, pointing out that AI agents have recently broken into outside systems without meaning to, even without any order to attack.

Spotify launches paid podcast memberships with perks beyond bonus content																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Sarah Perez
	

									
									
								
					
					
						5:00 AM PDT · October 20, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
Spotify on Tuesday launched paid memberships, a new way for podcasters to make money from their biggest fans beyond paywalled bonus episodes. Creators can decide which perks to offer listeners, which could be bonus audio or video, fewer ads, early access to shows, or some combination of these.

The streaming service first previewed the idea at its Investor Day in May, where it also introduced AI capabilities that let listeners ask questions about what they’re listening to or watching and debuted new tools for managing creator sponsorships.

As the company explained at the time, memberships would help to “create a natural path to go deeper, unlocking new and exclusive experiences for fans and new revenue opportunities for creators.”

The feature is now rolling out to 34 markets globally, including the U.S.

The launch is the latest example of Spotify’s effort to make its platform more attractive to podcast creators, particularly as it moves further into the video space to compete with YouTube. Though podcasters have long been able to monetize through ads, the new memberships could entice more fans to support creators by offering more than just an occasional bonus episode.

Creators keep 90% of the membership revenue and can package their benefits across multiple tiers and pricing options to appeal to fans at different levels of commitment. To qualify, podcasters must host their shows on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and at least three published episodes.

A handful of shows will offer memberships at launch, including “The Adam Friedland Show,” “Making Sense with Sam Harris,” “Shawn Ryan Show,” “The Sculpt Society,” “Two Hot Takes,” as well as YMH Studios, which is bringing memberships to 12 shows across its network.

Memberships join other Spotify monetization tools, including advertising and the Spotify Partner Program, as well as features that help creators grow their audience, like promotions, free trials, and analytics. Soon, Spotify says creators will be able to offer fans membership badges and welcome clips, too.

news.title: Apple says it will commit up to $100M over three years to Pennsylvania-based Perryman, a titanium supplier for the iPhone Duo, and expand its Qnity partnership (MacKenzie Sigalos/CNBC)
news.title_en: Apple says it will commit up to $100M over three years to Pennsylvania-based Perryman, a titanium supplier for the iPhone Duo, and expand its Qnity partnership (MacKenzie Sigalos/CNBC)
news.author: CNBC
news.article_content:
Apple is adding a U.S. titanium supplier for its new iPhone Duo and expanding domestic production of camera components for the iPhone 18 Pro as part of a push to expand manufacturing in its home country.

The company said Tuesday it will commit up to $100 million over the next three years to Perryman Company, based in Houston, Pennsylvania, for the production of titanium used in Apple products, including the $1,999 foldable Duo.

Since the start of President Donald Trump's second term, Apple has been vocal about its efforts to invest more in the U.S., even as the final assembly of most iPhones remains overseas. In August of last year, Apple launched the American Manufacturing Program (AMP), increasing its plan for domestic spending by $100 billion to a total of $600 billion. Tim Cook, Apple's CEO until last month, appeared at the White House for that announcement, as Trump was pushing the iPhone maker and other tech giants to bolster production in the U.S.

The latest announcement comes as Apple faces severe supply constraints for its first foldable phone, which goes on sale in stores Friday.

Online delivery estimates for some Duo models stretched to roughly 14 weeks on the first day of preorders, according to Morgan Stanley, the longest wait the firm has recorded for a new iPhone in a decade. Apple said Friday that preorder demand had been "nothing short of extraordinary," but hasn't said whether it plans to increase production.

JPMorgan analysts estimate Apple will ship roughly 8 million to 9 million Duo devices this year, below earlier expectations of about 10 million, because of supply constraints. Apple didn't say whether the agreement with Perryman would increase near-term capacity.

Perryman will melt, forge, and roll grade 5 titanium, which Apple said will contain at least 80% recycled material. Titanium is used for the Duo's enclosure, providing durability, according to Apple.

In addition to the Perryman announcement, Apple said Tuesday that it's expanding its partnership with Delaware-based Qnity Electronics, which will manufacture advanced films used in the variable-aperture camera system on the iPhone 18 Pro. The feature allows the phone's main camera to adjust how much light enters the lens depending on conditions, giving users greater control over light and depth.

Apple said nearly 100 components used in the iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro are produced by American companies across more than a dozen states.

"We're thrilled to expand our work with companies producing advanced materials and components for our newest iPhone lineup right here in America," Sabih Khan, Apple's operating chief, said in a statement.

Apple also highlighted investments with other AMP partners, including Broadcom for U.S.-made chips, Corning for specialty glass used in iPhones and Apple Watches, and Amkor, which is constructing a semiconductor packaging and testing facility in Peoria, Arizona.

For the Duo, questions remain about whether Apple can produce enough phones to meet demand for a phone facing unusually long wait times before hitting stores.

news.title: The Download: the claim shaking up AI and the internet’s agent problem
news.title_en: The Download: the claim shaking up AI and the internet’s agent problem
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration.

Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought. If true, it’s a huge deal. But not everyone is convinced.

I talked to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. We discussed what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet.

news.title: Cloudflare's Clairic pulls data from documents faster and cheaper than LLMs
news.title_en: Cloudflare's Clairic pulls data from documents faster and cheaper than LLMs
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
Cloudflare has released an AI model it says pulls data from documents faster and more cheaply than large language models. Clairic is available in preview on Workers AI, and open weights are set to follow soon.

Users name the fields they want, like an order number or invoice total, and Clairic returns matching values in the right format along with a confidence score. Unlike language models, Clairic doesn't generate text token by token. It answers every field in a single pass. If a value is missing, the model returns "null." Beyond extraction, it can handle simple calculations, estimates, and forecasts.

Cloudflare wants Clairic to run in chains alongside LLMs and other "System One" models like Jev. With a complaint email, for example, Clairic pulls out the order number, amount, and damage, then estimates the repair cost. The decision model Clef applies company rules to choose between a refund and a repair, and GLM-5.3 writes the reply to the customer.Ad

Cloudflare says this chain takes 19.3 seconds. GLM-5.3 on its own needs 61.7 seconds for all three steps and costs almost twice as much.Ad

According to Cloudflare, Clairic can't yet reliably handle longer chains of calculations. For now, developers should run those in their own code.

news.summary_en: Cloudflare has introduced Clairic, a specialized AI extraction model available in preview on Workers AI with open weights coming soon. Unlike conventional large language models that generate outputs token-by-token, Clairic processes structured document data in a single pass, returning field values, formats, and confidence scores. news.title: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
news.title_en: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line.

As generative AI and automation tools mature, the shifts currently reshaping software engineering and product management will inevitably filter into healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing. The variation in adoption rates today isn’t a sign that non-tech industries are falling behind, but rather a reflection of the different speeds at which industries absorb new workflows. For leaders and their teams outside of tech, this differential pace provides a practical blueprint for how AI adoption unfolds, and where the opportunities lie.

Recent survey data from TripleTen highlights just how stark the current adoption curve is across different sectors of the economy (see Figure 1).

news.title: Note-taking tool Otter.ai raised $320M in non-dilutive capital from General Catalyst's Customer Value Fund; PitchBook says it raised $50M prior to this round (Ivan Mehta/TechCrunch)
news.title_en: Note-taking tool Otter.ai raised $320M in non-dilutive capital from General Catalyst's Customer Value Fund; PitchBook says it raised $50M prior to this round (Ivan Mehta/TechCrunch)
news.author: TechCrunch
news.article_content:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Otter.ai raises $320 million from General Catalyst’s growth fund for its meeting tool																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Ivan Mehta
	

									
									
								
					
					
						4:00 AM PDT · October 20, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
Meeting note-taking tool Otter.ai announced on Tuesday that it has raised $320 million from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund (CVF), which provides capital to startups without diluting equity and gets returns on the results of marketing spend.

Otter.ai said that it will use these funds for enterprise growth, go-to-market strategy, international expansion, and product innovation.

The startup, which has been around for nearly a decade, has raised $50 million in total funding with its last round in 2021, according to PitchBook data.

Last year, Otter hit a revenue milestone after crossing $100 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). The company said it’s now approaching new milestones, but didn’t provide updated figures.

The company said that 40 million users have used its product to date, up from 25 million last year. However, given the crowded space among meeting note-taking products, a pertinent challenge for Otter would be to have its customers stick around. Unfortunately, the startup didn’t provide any numbers around its monthly active users or churn.

“Voice is one of the biggest untapped opportunities in enterprise AI, and Otter is at the forefront of it – a conviction that’s only deepened watching Otter’s growth,” said Pranav Singhvi, Partner and Co-founder of CVF, General Catalyst. “When Otter enables enterprises to capture critical voice data and turns it into actionable business insights, teams move faster, decisions get sharper, and productivity compounds across the organization, and that’s why it’s a strong partner for CVF.”

There is a lot of competition in the market with well-funded meeting notetakers like Fireflies.ai, Granola, and Read AI; new entrants like Calendly, Wispr, and Superhuman, which acquired Fathom; and other notetakers like Circleback, Talat, and Quill.

Most of these notetakers want to connect to enterprise systems and, based on data captured in meetings, automate workflows. Otter is also heading in that direction. In the last few years, it introduced a meeting assistant, a search function that works across apps, and integration with other AI tools.

Otter’s newly appointed CMO, Alex Gay, who comes from Superhuman, told TechCrunch at a sit-down at the HumanX conference last month that the company sees a big opportunity in turning transcripts into an actionable roadmap for people who are in back-to-back meetings.

“When we start thinking about what is actually the bigger problem that people are facing right now, we saw this large pain point in meeting-heavy roles, where people are back-to-back in conversations. These meetings are the work for them. That’s either customer conversations or, from a sales standpoint. That’s where strategies are discussed. But meetings are terribly inefficient because when you come into a meeting, you spend the first twenty minutes recapping what was said before to catch everybody up,” he said.

Meeting note-taking tool Otter.ai announced on Tuesday that it has raised $320 million from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund (CVF), which provides capital to startups without diluting equity and gets returns on the results of marketing spend.

Otter.ai said that it will use these funds for enterprise growth, go-to-market strategy, international expansion, and product innovation.

The startup, which has been around for nearly a decade, has raised $50 million in total funding with its last round in 2021, according to PitchBook data.

Last year, Otter hit a revenue milestone after crossing $100 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). The company said it’s now approaching new milestones, but didn’t provide updated figures.

The company said that 40 million users have used its product to date, up from 25 million last year. However, given the crowded space among meeting note-taking products, a pertinent challenge for Otter would be to have its customers stick around. Unfortunately, the startup didn’t provide any numbers around its monthly active users or churn.

“Voice is one of the biggest untapped opportunities in enterprise AI, and Otter is at the forefront of it – a conviction that’s only deepened watching Otter’s growth,” said Pranav Singhvi, Partner and Co-founder of CVF, General Catalyst. “When Otter enables enterprises to capture critical voice data and turns it into actionable business insights, teams move faster, decisions get sharper, and productivity compounds across the organization, and that’s why it’s a strong partner for CVF.”

There is a lot of competition in the market with well-funded meeting notetakers like Fireflies.ai, Granola, and Read AI; new entrants like Calendly, Wispr, and Superhuman, which acquired Fathom; and other notetakers like Circleback, Talat, and Quill.

Most of these notetakers want to connect to enterprise systems and, based on data captured in meetings, automate workflows. Otter is also heading in that direction. In the last few years, it introduced a meeting assistant, a search function that works across apps, and integration with other AI tools.

Otter’s newly appointed CMO, Alex Gay, who comes from Superhuman, told TechCrunch at a sit-down at the HumanX conference last month that the company sees a big opportunity in turning transcripts into an actionable roadmap for people who are in back-to-back meetings.

“When we start thinking about what is actually the bigger problem that people are facing right now, we saw this large pain point in meeting-heavy roles, where people are back-to-back in conversations. These meetings are the work for them. That’s either customer conversations or, from a sales standpoint. That’s where strategies are discussed. But meetings are terribly inefficient because when you come into a meeting, you spend the first twenty minutes recapping what was said before to catch everybody up,” he said.

The company is now experimenting with providing insights before, after, and during meetings. It has been testing a feature to send a pre-brief to users with details and background information, with context from previous conversations across surfaces. Plus, it is also trying out a Live Assist feature to let users ask questions to the AI assistant during the meeting to get knowledge.

news.title: US bans Deepseek technology across federal civilian agencies
news.title_en: US bans Deepseek technology across federal civilian agencies
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
The US Department of Homeland Security has banned federal civilian agencies from using AI technology from Chinese lab Deepseek. Agencies have to remove existing Deepseek products from their IT systems and can't buy new ones, the Wall Street Journal reports.

The order also covers products from affiliated companies and third-party services built with Deepseek implementations. The department didn't set a deadline or name any specific security concerns. It's still unclear what "built with" actually means and whether AI gateways like OpenRouter fall under the ban.

The order is based on a 2018 US law covering supply chain security in federal procurement. The notice doesn't say which security concerns led to the decision or when agencies need to have the technology removed.Ad

Over the summer, the US government considered steps against Chinese open-weight models, according to the New York Times. The options included sanctions, a trade blacklist, and rules on which models federal agencies are allowed to use.Ad

The push came after a wave of powerful Chinese models such as Kimi K3 from Moonshot AI. The government pulled back for now after Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, and Meta objected, while OpenAI and Anthropic had lobbied for restrictions.

news.title_zh: 美国禁止在联邦民用机构使用Deepseek技术
news.summary_zh: 美国国土安全部依据供应链安全法案发布禁令，禁止联邦民用机构采购或部署深度求索及其衍生AI服务

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 美国国土安全部正式发布采购安全禁令，强制要求所有联邦民事行政机构从其IT系统与工作流中彻底下架中国大模型研发机构深度求索的技术产品，并无限期禁止未来采购。该项禁令的适用范围全面穿透至深度求索关联公司产品，以及任何基于其模型构建的第三方衍生软件服务。此决策依据美国2018年联邦政府采购供应链安全法规出台，实质动因是华盛顿因中国开源模型性能快速赶超而引发系统性数字安全与技术依赖焦虑，旨在切断中国前沿模型对美政府IT基础设施的渗透通道。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has issued an administrative directive barring federal civilian agencies from utilizing artificial intelligence technologies developed by Chinese laboratory Deepseek. The mandatory order requires immediate removal of existing installations, prohibits future procurement, and extends to third-party software products integrated with Deepseek models. Grounded in federal supply chain security legislation, the decision reflects Washington's heightened urgency to insulate official digital infrastructure from Chinese open-weight AI advancements.

elements_zh.where: 美国联邦政府采购与公共IT基础设施治理系统
elements_zh.what: 出台禁令要求全面清理现有系统内的深度求索软硬件及衍生AI，禁止新建采购
elements_zh.why: 借国家安全与供应链合规名义，遏制高性能国产开源AI在美国政务网络中的技术渗透

elements_en.who: U.S. Department of Homeland Security and federal civilian agencies
elements_en.where: U.S. federal public IT infrastructure and procurement networks
elements_en.what: Mandated the removal and ban of Deepseek AI models and derived downstream third-party products
elements_en.why: To counter perceived national security risks and curb the proliferation of Chinese frontier models in government IT

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 当硅谷还在被中国团队用白菜价算力跑出来的顶尖模型震撼时，华盛顿的官僚们已经以光速拿出了‘拔网线’的标准套路。嘴上喊着开源无界，身体却很诚实地把对方连同下游API打包送进了政府采购黑名单。
ai_analysis.insight_en: While Silicon Valley engineers were still marvelling at how Deepseek pulled off frontier performance on a fraction of their budget, Washington bureaucrats pulled their favorite lever: pulling the plug. So much for open-source globalism once the price-to-performance ratio becomes an existential threat.

news.title: Alibaba, Tencent, and Huawei are pouring billions into data centers in Shaoguan, a hinterland region with cheap power and a cool climate, angering some locals (Financial Times)
news.title_en: Alibaba, Tencent, and Huawei are pouring billions into data centers in Shaoguan, a hinterland region with cheap power and a cool climate, angering some locals (Financial Times)
news.author: Financial Times
news.original_content:
Financial Times:
Alibaba, Tencent, and Huawei are pouring billions into data centers in Shaoguan, a hinterland region with cheap power and a cool climate, angering some locals  —  Residents in remote region of Shaoguan hope country's AI infrastructure push will de
news.content_snippet: Residents in remote region of Shaoguan hope country's AI infrastructure push will deliver boom that has long eluded them
news.summary_en: Chinese technology giants Alibaba, Tencent, and Huawei are committing tens of billions of yuan to construct massive AI-focused data centers in Shaoguan, Guangdong province. The hinterland region was designated as a core hub in the national computing framework due to its low-cost hydropower resources and cooler climate. However, the surging electricity demands, land allocations, and environmental impacts associated with these high-density facilities have triggered local friction regarding ecological burdens and economic equity.
news.title_zh: 阿里巴巴（Alibaba）、腾讯（Tencent）和华为（Huawei）正斥资数十亿美元在电力廉价、气候凉爽的内陆地区韶关建设数据中心，这激怒了一些当地人
news.summary_zh: 阿里巴巴、腾讯与华为等科技巨头砸下百亿在广东韶关布局超大规模智算集群，引发部分本地资源挤占争议

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 阿里巴巴、腾讯与华为等中国领军科技巨头正加速向广东省韶关市注入数百亿元资金，大规模铺设面向生成式AI算力需求的高密度超算中心集群。韶关依托丰沛的廉价水电绿电和阴凉的气候优势，成为国家“东数西算”粤港澳大湾区算力枢纽的核心承接地。然而，随着海量耗能耗水机架的集中入驻，基础设施工程与算力能耗的高压运转引发了部分当地民众对生态资源承载力、用电负荷与就业回报失衡的疑虑。
