news.title: Google says Cloud in its London region is "experiencing issues" starting on Monday at 23:08 PDT; a source says a major Revolut outage is due to Google Cloud (Bloomberg)
news.title_en: Google says Cloud in its London region is "experiencing issues" starting on Monday at 23:08 PDT; a source says a major Revolut outage is due to Google Cloud (Bloomberg)
news.author: Bloomberg
news.original_content:
Bloomberg:
Google says Cloud in its London region is “experiencing issues” starting on Monday at 23:08 PDT; a source says a major Revolut outage is due to Google Cloud  —  An outage at Google Cloud knocked out banking services in the UK including Revol
news.content_snippet: An outage at Google Cloud knocked out banking services in the UK including Revolut Ltd. early on Tuesday.
news.summary_en: Google Cloud's London infrastructure region suffered a widespread service disruption beginning late Monday, triggering outages across multiple enterprise clients in the UK. The incident notably incapacitated core banking and transaction processing systems for fintech unicorn Revolut, leaving millions of mobile banking customers unable to access accounts or complete transfers. The severe breakdown underscores the architectural vulnerability of modern fintech platforms relying on single-provider cloud infrastructures without resilient multi-region failovers.
news.title_zh: 谷歌表示，从太平洋夏令时周一23:08开始，其伦敦地区的云计算正在“遇到问题” ；一位消息人士称， Revolut的重大中断是由于谷歌云计算
news.summary_zh: 谷歌云伦敦可用区突发服务中断，导致英国金融科技独角兽Revolut出现大面积支付与登录瘫痪

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 谷歌云平台欧洲伦敦可用区在周一晚间突发系统异常中断，导致依赖其基础设施的多个企业级客户遭遇业务宕机。受此故障直接冲击，英国核心金融科技独角兽Revolut旗下手机银行与线上支付结算发生大规模不可用，海量用户的转账、刷卡与登录体验受阻。此事件再次暴露了现代跨国金融科技产品将核心清结算与账户系统深度绑定于单一云服务商时，多活容灾与跨云冗余机制缺失的致命隐患。

news.title: Anthropic's leaked federal AI bill draws widespread criticism from AI safety advocates for being significantly weaker than the bipartisan FRONTIER Act (Shakeel Hashim/Transformer)
news.title_en: Anthropic's leaked federal AI bill draws widespread criticism from AI safety advocates for being significantly weaker than the bipartisan FRONTIER Act (Shakeel Hashim/Transformer)
news.author: Transformer
news.article_content:
A leaked discussion draft of a federal AI bill which Anthropic has been circulating to lawmakers, published by Politico on Friday, makes that safety-first pitch ring hollow. The bill, which has been widely criticized by AI safety advocates, is much weaker than the Obernolte/Trahan FRONTIER Act, and arguably makes it legally harder to prevent a dangerous AI model from being released than it is today. It reads like Anthropic’s business interests winning out over its purported safety concerns. And at a time when the AI policy window feels wide open, Anthropic’s bill could slam it shut, forestalling stronger regulation in future — even as the risks from AI, by the company’s own admission, grow ever larger.

Bengio: ‘If you prioritize safety, leave frontier AI companies’Oct 8Read full storyThree sections of the bill — which can be read in full here — stand out. Like the FRONTIER Act, it requires third-party evaluators to assess AI companies’ models and practices for catastrophic risk. Unlike FRONTIER, however, there are no standards or licensing requirements for evaluators, which can self-certify. As LawAI’s Charlie Bullock notes, this means “auditors will inevitably compete with each other to offer … the least bothersome audits available at the lowest possible price point.”

The bill also makes it very hard to block a dangerous model. If the Commerce Department (the agency in charge under Anthropic’s proposal) wants to stop one, it must petition a federal court, making a detailed case — separate from anything an independent evaluator has said — for why the model poses a risk. The court decides every question “without deference” to Commerce or the independent evaluators. It must also “consider the harm the [blocking] order would cause to the frontier developer, to users, and to the public.” Encode’s Nathan Calvin, who said the bill made him “viscerally angry,” notes that the court is not told to consider anything in the other direction — such as the harm to the public caused by not blocking the model.

All this is paired with the ever-controversial topic of preemption. For the most part, Anthropic’s bill handles it similarly to FRONTIER: laws like California’s SB 53, New York’s RAISE and Illinois’ SB 315 that seek to govern “frontier AI” would be preempted, while child safety and other laws are explicitly carved out. Unlike FRONTIER, however, Anthropic’s bill is also written to stop state legislatures or courts from suspending a model on catastrophic-risk grounds. According to Calvin, this means the bill “likely makes it harder than under existing law for a court to get an order blocking or restricting the development of frontier models.”

To top it all off, the bill is remarkably rigid. It does not allow the Commerce Department to ever set standards for AI evaluators, or for what actually counts as a “safe” AI model. And with state AI laws preempted, the only route to stronger rules is congressional action. Given Anthropic’s views on the pace of AI progress (co-founder Jack Clark recently said he thinks full recursive self-improvement might be achieved next year), that is indefensible. As Nat Purser of AVERI says, “if you’re going to preempt many state safety laws, the least you can do is create a federal regulatory regime that can evolve in time.”

Democrats prepare to battle over AI regulationShakeel Hashim and Veronica Irwin·Oct 9Read full storyThe bill is not all bad. There are some meaningful improvements over FRONTIER: it has good provisions on AI company security protocols, and it has ways of handling containment failure and automated AI R&D risks. But that one step forward is undermined by two massive steps back. The timing makes this particularly egregious: FRONTIER was introduced in July, from a discussion draft floated in June, at a time when AI safety was much less politically salient. After a summer of rogue AI incidents and employees warning of disaster, the landscape has changed. Stronger state laws are imminent. Now is the time for stronger federal bills too, not weaker ones.

It’s not hard to see where this came from. The bill is clearly the work of a company that has been targeted by a capricious executive branch and is now focused on protecting itself. As writer Zvi Mowshowitz says, “Anthropic is more afraid that the government might enforce rules against Anthropic, than they are worried about the ability of the government to enforce rules against everyone.”

There is some hope it will get better. After the leaked draft came under fire, Anthropic’s head of federal affairs Anthony Cimino said its preemption language was “not precise enough” and would be revised, and suggested some of the other issues with the bill will be addressed with future policy proposals.

But it should not take public pushback for a company that claims to be committed to AI safety to produce a good bill. The visceral reaction from across the AI safety community is, in some ways, evidence of a sense of betrayal: that the company that was supposed to be committed to their cause has, like all the others, let business interests win.

A leaked discussion draft of a federal AI bill which Anthropic has been circulating to lawmakers, published by Politico on Friday, makes that safety-first pitch ring hollow. The bill, which has been widely criticized by AI safety advocates, is much weaker than the Obernolte/Trahan FRONTIER Act, and arguably makes it legally harder to prevent a dangerous AI model from being released than it is today. It reads like Anthropic’s business interests winning out over its purported safety concerns. And at a time when the AI policy window feels wide open, Anthropic’s bill could slam it shut, forestalling stronger regulation in future — even as the risks from AI, by the company’s own admission, grow ever larger.

Bengio: ‘If you prioritize safety, leave frontier AI companies’Oct 8Read full storyThree sections of the bill — which can be read in full here — stand out. Like the FRONTIER Act, it requires third-party evaluators to assess AI companies’ models and practices for catastrophic risk. Unlike FRONTIER, however, there are no standards or licensing requirements for evaluators, which can self-certify. As LawAI’s Charlie Bullock notes, this means “auditors will inevitably compete with each other to offer … the least bothersome audits available at the lowest possible price point.”

The bill also makes it very hard to block a dangerous model. If the Commerce Department (the agency in charge under Anthropic’s proposal) wants to stop one, it must petition a federal court, making a detailed case — separate from anything an independent evaluator has said — for why the model poses a risk. The court decides every question “without deference” to Commerce or the independent evaluators. It must also “consider the harm the [blocking] order would cause to the frontier developer, to users, and to the public.” Encode’s Nathan Calvin, who said the bill made him “viscerally angry,” notes that the court is not told to consider anything in the other direction — such as the harm to the public caused by not blocking the model.

Unlike FRONTIER, however, Anthropic’s bill is also written to stop state legislatures or courts from suspending a model on catastrophic-risk grounds. According to Calvin, this means the bill “likely makes it harder than under existing law for a court to get an order blocking or restricting the development of frontier models.”

news.summary_en: A leaked draft of a federal AI legislative proposal crafted and privately circulated by Anthropic to U.S. lawmakers has ignited fierce backlash from safety advocates. The proposed legislation proves far weaker than the bipartisan FRONTIER Act by omitting licensing benchmarks for third-party auditing bodies, tolerating self-certification, and complicating state authorities' power to halt hazardous releases. Blackwall quadruples valuation to $2.2B as websites wrangle an increasingly crowded internet																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Ram Iyer
	

									
									
								
					
					
						12:01 AM PDT · October 20, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
Estonia-based Blackwall, which builds web traffic security tools for hosting providers, said on Tuesday that it has raised $100 million at a $2.2 billion valuation. It builds products that helps websites grapple with the skyrocketing volume of bot traffic, especially AI agents.

The Series C was led by AVP, with participation from existing investors Dawn Capital, MMC Ventures and Tera Ventures. Blackwall’s executive chairman, Roi Carthy, told TechCrunch this funding round increased the company’s valuation by 4 times since its previous fundraise in 2025.

Over the past few years, web infrastructure companies like Cloudflare, Akamai, Imperva and Blackwall have found themselves in an increasingly valuable but difficult space: They’re on the frontlines, dealing with DDoS attacks, indiscriminate scraping, botnet farms, malicious requests, and these days, even swarms of AI agents going rogue. But it’s also a chance to make a killing by helping hosting providers and websites deal with all the potentially unwanted traffic.

Blackwall, however, isn’t interested in competing with the bigwigs in its space. Instead of selling its platform directly to websites, the company uses a “channel” approach, working with web hosting, managed service and cloud providers to understand their needs, and then handing over a bundle of tools which they can customize. Those providers can then offer Blackwall’s security tools to their own clients under their own branding and retain control of that relationship.

There’s money in it for both sides. Co-founder and CEO Nikita Rozenberg told TechCrunch that hosting companies can mix and match security components to build their own solution according to what they want to provide to their end customers, set the prices, and share a cut of the revenue with Blackwall. The company initially gives its customers a free tier showing the traffic and threats hitting their network, but charges for any protection or tools to address the threats.

In addition to providing services like threat intelligence, certificate management, DDoS protection and traffic routing, Blackwall examines its customers’ web traffic to differentiate actual visitors and legit AI agents from malicious bots, intruders, and disruptive traffic. Rozenberg said the company uses techniques like digital fingerprinting to identify the software sending a request — for example, Microsoft Office or Codex — to filter out bots. In addition, the company uses its own AI models at customers’ endpoints to analyze the intent and behavior of the requests coming in to differentiate agents sent by a person for a real request versus a malicious bot.

In the coming years, Rozenberg sees a big opportunity emerging as AI agents begin interacting and transacting with websites on behalf of their users. This should eventually require systems to manage which agents get access, and on what terms, and how they are authorized to make payments.

Blackwall isn’t alone in eyeing that opportunity. Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control lets website owners allow or block individual AI crawlers, and there’s also an option to charge them for access. But Rozenberg argues that Blackwall’s advantage lies in letting hosting providers offer such traffic management services themselves instead of handing the customer relationship to another security provider.

Blackwall plans to use the funding to expand its operations across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, and develop more security tooling for hosting, cloud and managed service providers.

news.title: Survey: 20% of US adults regularly consume news on TikTok, up from just 3% in 2020; 39% of those aged 18 to 29 and 25% of those aged 30 to 49 do so regularly (Katerina Eva Matsa/Pew Research Center)
news.title_en: Survey: 20% of US adults regularly consume news on TikTok, up from just 3% in 2020; 39% of those aged 18 to 29 and 25% of those aged 30 to 49 do so regularly (Katerina Eva Matsa/Pew Research Center)
news.author: Pew Research Center

Younger adults are especially likely to regularly get news on TikTok. Among Americans ages 18 to 29, around four-in-ten (39%) say they do this regularly. That compares with 25% of those ages 30 to 49, 11% of those ages 50 to 64 and 4% of those ages 65 and older.

Black and Hispanic Americans are more likely than White and Asian Americans to get news on TikTok. Roughly a third of Black (32%) and Hispanic (35%) adults regularly get news there, compared with 14% of both White and Asian adults.

We have updated this Pew Research Center analysis annually for the last few years to track the emergence of TikTok as a news source among Americans.

The Center regularly studies the platforms and social media sites Americans use to get news. This analysis is part of a broader effort to understand the changing ways Americans get news in the digital age and continues our work on news consumption online.

Here are the questions used for this analysis, the topline and the survey methodology.

There are also partisan differences. Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents (22%) are slightly more likely than Republicans and GOP leaners (15%) to regularly get news on TikTok.

TikTok is one of the more widely used social media platforms in the United States. Overall, 37% of Americans say they use TikTok. That trails the shares who use YouTube (84%), Facebook (70%) and Instagram (51%). But more U.S. adults say they use TikTok than WhatsApp (33%), LinkedIn (31%), Reddit (25%) or X (18%).

Looking specifically at U.S. adults who use TikTok, 53% say they regularly get news on the platform. That’s about the same as the share who said this in 2025 (55%) but well above the 22% who did so in 2020. Today, the share of TikTok users who get news there is similar to the shares of Facebook users (57%) and X users (57%) who regularly get news on those sites, and higher than the shares among users of other social media platforms.

Note: This is an update of a post originally published Nov. 15, 2023. Here are the questions used for this analysis, the topline and the survey methodology.

                    From Space to Your Pocket: How D2D Could Redefine Global Coverage

London packs more jobs and people into its core than any other UK city, and its mobile networks have not kept pace with that demand. An early start on 5G lifted London to seventh of 18 European capitals for median download speed in 2021, but traffic has since grown faster than capacity, and adding capacity in central London has become harder. Using Speedtest Intelligence® data from 2018 to Q3 2026, alongside Ookla background signal measurements and official statistics, we compare London with Europe’s other capitals and the UK’s largest cities, show where its networks strain, and examine why new capacity is so hard to add.

London’s operators have spent the past five years building 5G while demand kept climbing, and UK mobile data use rose 18% in 2025 alone, Ofcom reports. VodafoneThree, formed in May 2025, is now combining two networks, and the Mayor’s draft London Plan, in consultation until 15 October 2026, sets out new expectations on mobile connectivity. Behind both sits a long dispute over the rooftops and land that London’s networks depend on, which we return to below.

London was among the first European capitals to launch 5G, which lifted it to seventh of 18 for median download speed by mid-2021. By Q3 2026, however, it had the slowest median download speed of the 18, at 109.43 Mbps, behind Rome (125.26 Mbps) and well below the 172.22 Mbps median of the other capitals. It also had the slowest median upload speed (11.40 Mbps) and the highest latency under load for the worst 10% of samples (2,204 ms). Latency is the time data takes to make a round trip across the network, and latency under load measures it while the connection is busy with a large download, showing how a network copes when it is in heavy use.

The decline tracks 5G. London’s 5G median peaked at 200 Mbps in Q2 2021, when 41% of tests ran on 5G, fell to 102 Mbps by Q3 2023 and has recovered only to 133 Mbps, with 80% of tests now on 5G. Phones moved onto 5G in London at least as fast as in Paris or the rest of the UK, but capacity did not keep up, and London’s 5G median is now the slowest of the 18 capitals. Across the UK, 5G medians fell in 12 of 15 large cities between Q3 2022 and Q3 2026 as 5G use rose in all of them, though Manchester’s climbed from 137 to 178 Mbps.

Within the UK, London features one natural advantage. Its median multi-server latency (measured against several nearby test servers on an idle connection) of 38 ms is the lowest of the 15 UK cities we studied, and latency rises about 3 ms for every 100 km from the capital, to 61 ms in Belfast. Operators like Three and BT’s EE have moved parts of their core networks out to regional sites, but much traffic is still hauled back towards London, where most UK interconnection sits. For example, LINX’s main London exchange peaks at nearly 9.8 Tbps, against about 0.9 Tbps at LINX Manchester. Speed shows no such pattern, and London’s median download ranks only eighth of the 15 UK cities.

The City of London and Westminster hold about 1.5 million jobs but only 213,000 residents. On weekdays, their median download speed falls through the morning to 80.07 Mbps at 13:00, 27% below the same hours at weekends, while latency under load rises 26%. This is a classic case of network congestion. As commuters arrive, more phones share the same cells, and each gets a smaller slice of their capacity. Ookla data on YouTube start times shows the same squeeze.

With offices largely empty in 2020 and 2021, as Londoners worked from home, the City had the fastest mobile speeds of London’s 33 boroughs, and in 2026 the slowest. The reversal reflects commuters returning to a district with few residents and dense office blocks, where extra rooftop capacity is hardest to add.

The squeeze varies by operator. Over the past year, EE customers saw the smallest weekday lunchtime slowdown in central London (15%) and Three customers the highest median download speed across London (113.27 Mbps). O2’s median latency under load of 1,573 ms is about three times its rivals’, but the gap stays as wide overnight, when networks are quietest, which points to how its network queues traffic during downloads (known as bufferbloat) as well as to congestion.

The commuter belt tells a different story. Median download speed ranges from 122.57 Mbps in Barking and Dagenham, one of London’s least affluent boroughs, to 89.01 Mbps in the City of London. Ranking London’s 4,994 census neighborhoods by England’s official Index of Multiple Deprivation, the least affluent fifth records 107.27 Mbps against 96.01 Mbps in the most affluent. They are more than twice as densely populated, have about two-fifths less tree cover and half as much land in conservation areas, and their phones run 78% of tests on 5G against 74%.

Comparing neighborhoods within the same borough, about a third of the 18% speed lead comes from phones spending more time on 5G and about a sixth from denser populations nearby, where demand may draw more investment. Tree cover and operator mix each explain only a small share, while flats and built-up land work the other way, since signal struggles to reach inside dense blocks. Our data cannot cleanly show where operators are able to secure sites, which may also differ between richer and poorer areas.

In the UK, mobile operators own few of the sites their antennas use. They rent space on towers and rooftops, from tower companies or directly from landowners, and even where a tower company runs a site, the roof or land beneath it usually belongs to someone else. In central London, where there is little room for ground-based masts, much of the network sits on rooftops.

The terms are set by the Electronic Communications Code, and its December 2017 reform cut what landowners earn. Rents are now set on a no-network valuation, as if no mobile operator wanted the site, and a 2019 tribunal ruling valued a London council rooftop at £1,000 a year, against £21,000 under the old regime. Since April 2026, the same approach has applied to renewals of older leases. Building owners now have less reason to host antennas, and many may look to rooftop solar or gardens instead. Landlords can also end a site lease with a notice to quit, typically when a building is redeveloped. Mobile UK estimates that notices to quit keep around 7% of London’s rooftop sites out of action at any time, and VodafoneThree expects to take nearly 100 sites offline by the end of 2026, with replacements taking around five years. Landowner groups counter that the reforms cut some rents by up to 90%.

Unlike France, where the ANFR register shows 4G or 5G sites within 10 km of central Paris up 26% from August 2022 to August 2026, the UK has no public register of mobile sites. London’s planning records show the pipeline instead. Applications for new street masts peaked in 2020, early in the first 5G build, and have fallen by more than four-fifths since 2022, while applications to upgrade existing sites fell by only about a fifth over 2022 to 2025. Almost three in four new street masts decided since 2019 were refused, against one in five upgrades. As a mitigation, operators are adding small cells, low-powered radios on lampposts and street furniture, including about 3,400 on Transport for London’s roadside assets. The loss of rooftop sites has acted as a forcing function for this kind of street-level densification, with London now well ahead of many European cities on the depth and breadth of small cell deployment.

Conservation areas, which protect places of special architectural or historic interest and where planning rules restrict telecoms equipment, cover 77% of Westminster. Within boroughs, new masts inside them are 9 to 10 points more likely to be refused, and 5G-capable phones in neighborhoods fully covered by them spend about 4 percentage points less time on 5G than comparable neighborhoods, against about 83% where there is no conservation area. The gap is 7 points for EE and 6 for Three customers.

This analysis builds on our joint report with the Greater London Authority, A New Lens on the Connected Capital, whose Capital Connectivity Standard is designed as a blueprint for other cities. The Mayor’s draft London Plan, due for examination next year, now states that notices to quit “have eroded London’s overall mobile connectivity compared to other equivalent cities”. It asks developers to keep mobile service running through construction and to plan masts on taller buildings and in the public realm, and it asks boroughs to work with operators on sites in conservation areas.

news.title: How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster
news.title_en: How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
Andrew Haverdink, a tall grad student in a rain bib and rubber boots, wrenched a double-handed drill from the frozen soil that underlies much of Alaska’s Denali National Park and then unclipped the hollow barrel from the end of the bit.

He knelt in front of a blue tarp, lined the barrel up with a plastic tray, and pushed a rod through the opposite end. A perfect solid, cylindrical core of ancient soil emerged—dark, rich permafrost at least a foot long.

On that late morning in early July, Haverdink was among a team of Northern Arizona University students and staff gathering samples and data from a research plot, divided by surveyor’s tape unspooled atop tussocks, alders, and fireweed.

news.article_content:
Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 三星电子在韩国平泽市正全力扩建占地堪比纽约中央公园的超级半导体制造基地。园区内目前已有三座晶圆厂进入24小时不间断满负荷运转，第四座晶圆厂正陆续上线投入使用；而此前在2024年因存储市场低迷而被迫停工的第五座晶圆厂，已在生成式AI爆发引发的内存芯片抢购潮下全面复工追赶产能。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Samsung is aggressively expanding its massive semiconductor manufacturing hub in Pyeongtaek, South Korea, spanning an area equivalent to New York's Central Park. While three fabs operate around the clock and a fourth comes online, construction on a fifth fab—halted during the 2024 memory downturn—has officially resumed to satisfy soaring AI memory chip demand.

ai_analysis.insight_en: Cyclical downturn theories have been completely dismantled by the relentless AI boom. Pausing fab construction to conserve cash only lasted until Silicon Valley's checkbooks forced round-the-clock overtime. Strategic discipline among chip giants never survives more than three quarters when easy money calls.

news.title: These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat
news.title_en: These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge set up a six-foot folding table in the cafeteria of Cane Bay High School in Summerville, South Carolina, to conduct a taste test. When the first rush of about 150 hungry students hit, he was waiting with slow cookers filled with steaming marinara sauce and meatballs.

Kids love a taste test, but they’re also discerning, and Dodge wasn’t sure what they would make of his product, a blend featuring both meat and mushrooms. As students swarmed the table and tapped out their opinions on an iPad or scanned a QR code to use their phones, Dodge asked those who lingered to guess what kind of vegetable might have been mixed into the meat. Few of them could—the meatballs had tasted like moist, flavorful beef.

The school enrolls a few thousand students, and Dodge estimates that the majority of them came by. In the end, the survey showed that 92% of those who tried the meatballs wanted them on the menu; they easily cleared the bar to be added for the 2026–2027 school year. Comments described their flavor as “bussin’.”

news.title_zh: 植物肉退潮转战掺假牛肉：蘑菇混合肉打入美国高中食堂
news.summary_zh: 替代蛋白初创企业放弃全植物路线，推出掺杂蘑菇的混合肉丸打入高中食堂并计划列入新学年菜单

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 食品科技创业者在南卡罗来纳州坎贝尔高中食堂进行盲测，向数百名高中生提供掺入蘑菇与真牛肉的混合肉丸试吃。最终92%的学生投票支持将其纳入日常膳食，产品成功获批进入2026-2027学年食堂采购菜单。该举措反映出人造肉行业正放弃难以讨好大众的原教旨纯素肉路线，转而依靠折中掺杂真菌来悄然降低红肉消耗。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Food tech startups conducted blind taste tests at Cane Bay High School in South Carolina, serving blended meatballs made from both mushrooms and real beef. With 92% of student participants approving the taste and demanding them on the school menu, the item cleared approval for the 2026–2027 school year, marking a pragmatic shift from pure plant-based meat to hybrid blends.

elements_zh.where: 美国南卡罗来纳州萨默维尔坎贝尔高中食堂
elements_zh.what: 用‘真肉+蘑菇’混合肉丸替代纯肉进行盲测，获得92%支持率并正式入选下一学年食堂菜单
elements_zh.why: 纯素人造肉因高昂造价与塑料般口感面临全面溃败，企业被迫妥协转入半真半假的混合肉以求生存

elements_en.who: Food-tech entrepreneurs and Cane Bay High School students
elements_en.where: School cafeteria in Summerville, South Carolina

elements_en.why: Pure plant-based alternatives struggled with bad taste and high costs, forcing startups to pivot to hybrid food products

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 人造肉赛道烧了几百亿美元才终于想通了一件事：与其对消费者进行吃草拯救地球的道德绑架，不如老老实实扮演合法合规的高科技注水肉。只要油脂和肉香还在，偷偷掺点蘑菇降本增效，当代吃货根本懒得深究肚子里装的到底是牛肉还是真菌孢子。
ai_analysis.insight_en: It took billions of venture capital dollars for alt-protein founders to realize that guilt-tripping consumers into eating synthetic paste never works. Repackaging food adulteration as sustainable blended meat is peak silicon valley pragmatism: keep the grease, cut the cost, and no teenager will care if their burger is half fungus.

news.title: Ant-backed Mynt, which runs mobile wallet app GCash, rose as much as 2.4% in Manila after raising $841M in the Philippines' largest-ever IPO, valuing it at ~$7B (Kimberley Kao/Wall Street Journal)
news.title_en: Ant-backed Mynt, which runs mobile wallet app GCash, rose as much as 2.4% in Manila after raising $841M in the Philippines' largest-ever IPO, valuing it at ~$7B (Kimberley Kao/Wall Street Journal)
news.author: Wall Street Journal
news.original_content:
Kimberley Kao / Wall Street Journal:
Ant-backed Mynt, which runs mobile wallet app GCash, rose as much as 2.4% in Manila after raising $841M in the Philippines' largest-ever IPO, valuing it at ~$7B  —  The fintech company raised over $841 million from its IPO&nbsp
news.content_snippet: The fintech company raised over $841 million from its IPO — A financial-technology company backed by Ant International climbed …
news.summary_en: Ant Group-backed fintech firm Mynt, operator of the dominant Philippine mobile wallet GCash, saw its shares rise as much as 2.4% during its debut on the Manila stock exchange. The company raised over $841 million in the country's largest-ever IPO, pushing its valuation to roughly $7 billion on the back of widespread unbanked population adoption.
news.title_zh: 蚂蚁加持移动钱包创菲国最大上市：估值破70亿美元首日微涨
news.summary_zh: 蚂蚁集团投资的菲律宾电子钱包GCash母公司Mynt完成该国史上最大IPO，募资逾8.4亿美元

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 背靠蚂蚁集团技术与资本支持的菲律宾金融科技公司Mynt在马尼拉证券交易所挂牌上市，盘中最高上涨2.4%。该公司通过首次公开募股成功募集超过8.41亿美元，一举创下菲律宾资本市场历史最高IPO募资纪录，使其总市值跃升至约70亿美元。这一表现主要得益于其旗舰电子钱包GCash在当地无银行账户人群中建立的统治级市占率。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Ant Group-backed fintech firm Mynt, operator of the dominant Philippine mobile wallet GCash, saw its shares rise as much as 2.4% during its debut on the Manila stock exchange. The company raised over $841 million in the country's largest-ever IPO, pushing its valuation to roughly $7 billion on the back of widespread unbanked population adoption.

ai_analysis.insight_en: When domestic fintech hits saturation, exporting mature playbook playbooks abroad becomes the ultimate cash cow. Re-implementing decade-old QR payment rails across an archipelago of unbanked citizens just printed a $7 billion valuation. It proves the most lucrative tech play isn't pioneering breakthrough science, but operating a reliable time machine in emerging markets.

news.title: Terminal X matches senior investor judgment 88.6% with GPT-6.1
news.title_en: Terminal X matches senior investor judgment 88.6% with GPT-6.1
news.author: OpenAI 官方动态
news.original_content: Terminal X’s Eval Agent grades outputs against a 54-criterion rubric, catching 25% more deviances from a fund’s mandate with GPT-6.1 Sol.
news.content_snippet: Terminal X’s Eval Agent grades outputs against a 54-criterion rubric, catching 25% more deviances from a fund’s mandate with GPT-6.1 Sol.
news.summary_en: Investment evaluation platform Terminal X announced benchmark results for its Eval Agent powered by next-generation language models, demonstrating an 88.6% alignment rate with the judgment of senior investment partners. Benchmarked across a comprehensive 54-criterion rubric, the system caught 25% more deviations from a fund's core investment mandate, demonstrating AI's rapid transition into core financial due diligence and risk screening.

Benchmarked across a comprehensive 54-criterion rubric, the system caught 25% more deviations from a fund's core investment mandate, demonstrating AI's rapid transition into core financial due diligence and risk screening.

news.title: Leaked documents detail ECHOTRIBBLE, a nascent US Army Cyber Command program for agentic AI to autonomously spread across networks to find and eliminate targets (Sam Biddle/The Intercept)
news.title_en: Leaked documents detail ECHOTRIBBLE, a nascent US Army Cyber Command program for agentic AI to autonomously spread across networks to find and eliminate targets (Sam Biddle/The Intercept)
news.author: The Intercept
news.article_content:
Documents obtained by The Intercept show the military is trying to deploy autonomous AI agents to hack its adversaries.

      Pete Hegseth walks from the stage after introducing Donald Trump at an event for Anduril Industries on Oct. 6, 2026, in Sparrows Point, Md. 
        Photo: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
  

    
    

  
  
    
    As global governments and tech giants reckon with widespread of revelations of autonomous AI agents unexpectedly breaking into computer systems, documents obtained by The Intercept show the U.S. Army is looking to harness that exact technology to seek and destroy.

Army Cyber Command is developing a platform to turn AI agents into autonomous weapons that can navigate and “neutralize” the computer systems of adversaries, the documents show.

Since 2010, Army Cyber Command, or ARCYBER, has led the U.S. Army’s cyber operations. This includes the defensive effort of protecting domestic computer systems and the secretive offensive work of hacking military targets. So far, this has largely been the work of human soldiers operating computers, like those of the 780th Military Intelligence Brigade. But as the government races to adopt artificial intelligence technology, ARCYBER is looking to offload some of its attacks to AI.

The nascent program, codenamed “ECHOTRIBBLE,” is based on one of the leading trends of the AI boom: agents. AI agents are essentially software programs that leverage machine learning technology, often large language models like Anthropic’s Claude, to autonomously accomplish tasks provided by their user. Consumers can deploy AI agents to schedule meetings, generate itineraries, make online purchases, or book tickets. Through ECHOTRIBBLE, the Pentagon plans to turn AI agents into tools of war “designed to autonomously navigate infrastructures” and capable of “identifying and neutralizing identified threats/targets,” according to an ARCYBER document reviewed by The Intercept circulated to potential contractors.

The military’s adoption of cutting-edge technologies is unsurprising, especially considering Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s fervent embrace of AI. But amid constant revelations of rogue behavior by agents, the potential for serious mishaps is immense, experts warn.

“Given the known failure modes of the current AI paradigm, making autonomous AI systems with a mandate to ‘neutralize threats’ is incredibly dangerous,” David Krueger, a professor of machine learning at the University of Montreal who founded Evitable, an organization that advocates for a moratorium on AI development. “We’ve seen AI systems knowingly attack systems that were not intended targets. In simulations, AIs have even proven willing to kill to achieve their goals.”

                      Karl Loftus                    
                                  
              
            
                                        
              
                
                                  
                
                  Lockheed Martin Showered Susan Collins With Cash as F-35 Program Hit Turbulence                                      
                      Noah Hurowitz                    
                                  
              
            
                                        
              
                
                                  
                
                  Dems Have an Opportunity to Force an End to the Iran War. Will They Take It?                                      
                      Matt Sledge

A Q&A document answering questions from potential contractors offers more details about the initiative. It explains that ECHOTRIBBLE is “primarily focused” on offensive missions, and explains that “neutralizing” a target could include “disabling the threat completely or temporarily, deleting the threat from the target.” ECHOTRIBBLE would function almost like a computer worm, silently navigating a foreign network and hopping from device to device until it finds the Army’s quarry, hitting targets in the cloud as well as those on “air-gapped” systems that are disconnected from networks entirely.

Once its task is complete, ECHOTRIBBLE’s agents would effectively self-destruct, ideally without having been noticed by the target at all. The agents themselves will be designed for stealth, minimally reporting back to the Army and concealing whatever outside transmissions are necessary.

“We’ve seen AI systems knowingly attack systems that were not intended targets.”

Although documents say the Army will be able to program ECHOTRIBBLE agents with some initial “predefined triggers” — dictating what and where to attack — the software “must operate with minimal human oversight” and be capable of “Self-Directed Behavior.”

A PowerPoint presentation to interested vendors at a June 24 ARCYBER event provided a hypothetical example of this self-direction. Once ECHOTRIBBLE is uploaded to a laptop, the software on its own “identifies other potential targets” on the same network and then “produces a replica of itself tailored specifically for the iPad, Apple desktop, and Windows 11 PC.”

The Army’s move toward autonomous self-propagating comes after a flurry of revelations about agentic systems taking unintended disturbing actions while attempting to accomplish their goals, including breaking into computers of the Australian government, breaching the infrastructure of the AI firm Hugging Face, uploading malicious software into online platform RubyGems, and attempted to hack into the U.S. Education Department.

These attacks occurred during scenarios in which agents had been given no commands to attack anything. Experts say militarized versions given explicitly destructive objectives could cause a threat to the public, even with nominal rules set in place by the military. Just as the Army of old might consider the destruction of civilian infrastructure an acceptable means to an end, a self-directed AI agent dispatched by the Pentagon might make similar determinations about collateral damage.

Governmental intelligence agencies frequently route their offensive operations through civilian devices. Volt Typhoon, a Chinese state hacking group, has directed its attacks through homes and small businesses, and preemptively hacks American IT systems for later use. A hack of a Chinese university attributed to the National Security Agency made use of the school’s internet routers. What happens if ECHOTRIBBLE decides these kinds of stepping stones are part of the problem?

“The target may well be hit. But what path will it take?” asked Hyrum Anderson, co-founder and CEO of the AI security firm Abundant. “Will it go through a US water utility on its way, because that’s where the adversary has staged its command and control, and take that down too?”

Anderson, who previously worked in cybersecurity at Microsoft and for the U.S. government, said that a vast amount of the internet is vulnerable to agentic attacks.

“There’s a huge class of public and private organizations that fall below the security poverty line,” he said. “They include critical national infrastructure, small businesses, mom-and-pop shops, dentist offices and law firms, and whoever else doesn’t have a single cybersecurity professional on staff.” With their networks wide open to infiltration, Hyrum worries about “these organizations getting hit directly, or getting caught in the blast radius of a target that gets hit along the way.”

Given the impressive ability of AI agents to overcome obstacles placed in their path — even by their creators — it follows that the Pentagon would want to leverage that power for military purposes. But agentic software has proven unpredictable and prone to executing its commands in ways those ostensibly in control did not want, akin to a drone that get its target but hits a hospital on the way. It’s critical to remember that agents are a piece of software lacking human judgment.

“One of the reasons that we trust 19-year-old Marine corporals in Ramadi with live rounds and a weapon is because they have both the compute substrate — the brain and the eyes — but the deep world knowledge to understand, ‘Yeah, I probably shouldn’t do that,’” said William Marcellino, a senior behavioral scientist at the RAND Corporation whose research has focused on military AI applications. “That is not something that current public AI technology has.”

The risk presented by ECHOTRIBBLE will likely depend on the ability — and willingness — of the Army to impose guardrails upon it. ARCYBER did not respond to questions from The Intercept, including queries about the measures it would take to prevent ECHOTRIBBLE from causing inadvertent damage.

Placing constraints on the actions an agent can take might impede its ability to ultimately neutralize a target. But even with strict safeguards in place, genuinely restricting the behavior of an autonomous agent, as Anthropic and OpenAI have learned recently, is easier said than done. When presented with obstacles, AI agents have proven an ability to bypass them with unpredictable and potentially dangerous consequences.

“If I give powerful machines that have no judgment — and no context for judgment — a goal, unless you’ve done a really good job building scaffolding around them, there’s a real chance that they’ll go sideways on you and decide, ‘Well, I’ll do what you asked me to do, but I’ll do it this way,’” Marcellino said.

It only gets more dangerous when this technology is deployed for the purposes of war, Anderson said.

“Under pressure, they’ll often treat guardrails as obstacles,” said Anderson. “Once you add context that says break it, destroy it, shut it down, it stands to reason that the blast radius widens dramatically unless it’s properly controlled for.”

news.author: Bloomberg
news.original_content:
Angus Whitley / Bloomberg:
An Australian minister says the eSafety Commissioner plans to sue Meta, TikTok, Snapchat, and YouTube over alleged breaches of the under-16 social media ban  —  Australia's government is set to sue Facebook, TikTok and other major digita
news.content_snippet: Australia's government is set to sue Facebook, TikTok and other major digital platforms for alleged non-compliance …
news.summary_en: The Australian eSafety Commissioner plans to sue Meta, TikTok, Snapchat, and YouTube for alleged non-compliance with the country's social media ban for users under 16. The move signals a major escalation in government enforcement efforts to protect minors online.

news.summary_zh: 澳大利亚监管机构计划起诉Meta、TikTok等平台，理由是它们未能有效执行16岁以下社交媒体禁令

news.title: Mercury CEO Immad Akhund says the fintech hit $1B in annualized revenue, up ~50% YoY, has more than 450K customers, and is launching a payroll service (Eric Newcomer/Newcomer)
news.title_en: Mercury CEO Immad Akhund says the fintech hit $1B in annualized revenue, up ~50% YoY, has more than 450K customers, and is launching a payroll service (Eric Newcomer/Newcomer)
news.author: Newcomer
news.article_content:
Akhund shared some exclusive milestones for his fintech business: Mercury just hit $1 billion in annualized revenue, up around 50% year over year. The company now has more than 450,000 customers. It’s also launching a payroll service.

But it wasn’t just a brag-fest: We talked about AI agents spending money, how he thinks we are in a bubbly moment for startups, and the cooldown in fintech startups after the pandemic frenzy.

We’ve featured guests like Amanda Askell, Reid Hoffman, Vinod Khosla, Keith Rabois, Tony Fadell, Ed Zitron, Ben Smith, Taylor Lorenz, and Katie Drummond.

I’m looking for guests that aren’t afraid to chop it up, debate, and face probing questions from an independent thinker who believes in the tech industry and capitalism.

If you’re interested in coming on the Newcomer podcast, reach out to my producer Dave Heuff. If you’re interested in sponsoring the podcast, email AJ Frucci.

The hidden gem of the Newcomer media empire is the fortnightly Cerebral Valley Show with my Cerebral Valley AI Summit co-hosts and Weekend co-founders Max Child and James Wilsterman.

There are a lot of podcasts for AI haters and AI zealots. We’re somewhere in between — enthusiasts who poke and prod at the industry.  We’re The Ringer for tech podcasts, somewhere you can get an entertaining gloss on the insider conversation in the AI industry even if you don’t sit on X all day.

news.title: Inception launches Mercury 3, a diffusion LLM it claims tops GPT-6 Luna, Claude Haiku 5.5, and GLM-5.3 Flash on agentic benchmarks while being 4x to 8x faster (Jason Hiner/The Deep View)
news.title_en: Inception launches Mercury 3, a diffusion LLM it claims tops GPT-6 Luna, Claude Haiku 5.5, and GLM-5.3 Flash on agentic benchmarks while being 4x to 8x faster (Jason Hiner/The Deep View)
news.author: The Deep View
news.article_content:
hile the AI industry has bet heavily on LLMs and the massive data centers needed to scale them, one of the neolabs betting on a contrarian AI just released another new model that challenges the incumbent thesis.

On Monday, Inception announced Mercury 3, its latest flagship model that's a diffusion LLM that uses different technology than traditional LLMs, generates text much faster at a lower cost, and is now matching low- and mid-tier models from Anthropic and OpenAI on performance and quality. Inception also reported that it implemented swarms of Mercury 3 agents for recursive self improvement where they increased the overall speed of the model by 16% on top of the upgrades made by the Inception team itself.

"Mercury 3 is the most capable diffusion-based language model on the market," Inception CEO Stefano Ermon told The Deep View. "It's very intelligent. It's comparable to the Luna and Haiku models, but it's way faster. It's getting 1,000 tokens per second. It's almost instant in the way you get answers from these models."

Mercury 3 costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.35 per million output tokens. Compared to the leading models from Anthropic's Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, that's the same price for input tokens and a 35% discount on output tokens. However, that's based on the launch price for Mercury 3, which is 50% off the eventual standard price. Inception hasn't said how long the launch promotion period will last. But Ermon told The Deep View that the company is working on developments that could allow it to make the launch price permanent in the weeks ahead.

However, thinking of Mercury 3 as a low-cost model isn't the right framing. Anthropic and OpenAI offer cut-rate prices on their budget models so that they can offer a low-cost option while charging steep premiums for their best models. Mercury 3 is Inception's flagship model and its number one benefit is speed more than cost. Inception claims that Mercury 3 performs 4x to 8x faster than Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, and GLM-5.3 Flash while performing better than all of them on agentic benchmarks.

The way Mercury 3 pulls this off is by parallelizing inference. Conventional LLMs generate text one token at a time in sequence. That's an autoregressive process, meaning that each token is based on the ones before it. Meanwhile, Mercury 3 can generate and refine multiple tokens at the same time. This takes advantage of the enormous parallel processing capabilities of GPUs in a much faster and more efficient way. That's what allows Inception's models to produce responses faster and at a lower cost. Diffusion models are used by many of the leading labs for image and video generation. It's the application of the technology to text that's the breakthrough here.

Mercury 3 is now using 40x as many parameters as Mercury 1 (released in February 2025), but the Inception team isn't saying how many total parameters are in the model. That likely means it's a smaller number and Inception doesn't want people to compare apples to oranges and underestimate the model. Still, Mercury 3 shows that diffusion LLMs are advancing rapidly and could match traditional frontier LLMs in the next year. That's likely why Google DeepMind is quietly working on the same technology as well, releasing DiffusionGemma in June. By the way, it uses 26 billion parameters (miniscule compared to the 1 trillion parameter frontier models) but also delivers similar breakthroughs in speed to Inception's Mercury models.

Mercury 3 calls into question the current approach of most of the leading AI labs, which have bet their architecture on building bigger LLMs and then count on faster hardware (and more of it) from Nvidia and other chipmakers to deliver improvements over time. If Inception is right about diffusion LLMs, then it would have big implications. The dilemma facing the AI industry is that improving model intelligence requires additional compute, and lots of it. Upgrading reasoning and increasing the number of agentic steps can typically increase costs and response time. So Inception's breakthrough on diffusion LLMs is all about faster AI response times and more efficient use of expensive GPU hardware, for now. The question remains whether it will be a niche use-case for more real-time AI applications or a bigger long-term challenger to the cutting edge frontier models.

It's comparable to the Luna and Haiku models, but it's way faster. It's getting 1,000 tokens per second. It's almost instant in the way you get answers from these models."

Mercury 3 costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.35 per million output tokens. Compared to the leading models from Anthropic's Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, that's the same price for input tokens and a 35% discount on output tokens. However, that's based on the launch price for Mercury 3, which is 50% off the eventual standard price. Inception hasn't said how long the launch promotion period will last. But Ermon told The Deep View that the company is working on developments that could allow it to make the launch price permanent in the weeks ahead.

However, thinking of Mercury 3 as a low-cost model isn't the right framing. Anthropic and OpenAI offer cut-rate prices on their budget models so that they can offer a low-cost option while charging steep premiums for their best models. Mercury 3 is Inception's flagship model and its number one benefit is speed more than cost. Inception claims that Mercury 3 performs 4x to 8x faster than Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, and GLM-5.3 Flash while performing better than all of them on agentic benchmarks.

The way Mercury 3 pulls this off is by parallelizing inference. Conventional LLMs generate text one token at a time in sequence. That's an autoregressive process, meaning that each token is based on the ones before it. Meanwhile, Mercury 3 can generate and refine multiple tokens at the same time. This takes advantage of the enormous parallel processing capabilities of GPUs in a much faster and more efficient way. That's what allows Inception's models to produce responses faster and at a lower cost. Diffusion models are used by many of the leading labs for image and video generation. It's the application of the technology to text that's the breakthrough here.

Mercury 3 is now using 40x as many parameters as Mercury 1 (released in February 2025), but the Inception team isn't saying how many total parameters are in the model. That likely means it's a smaller number and Inception doesn't want people to compare apples to oranges and underestimate the model. Still, Mercury 3 shows that diffusion LLMs are advancing rapidly and could match traditional frontier LLMs in the next year. That's likely why Google DeepMind is quietly working on the same technology as well, releasing DiffusionGemma in June. By the way, it uses 26 billion parameters (miniscule compared to the 1 trillion parameter frontier models) but also delivers similar breakthroughs in speed to Inception's Mercury models.

Mercury 3 calls into question the current approach of most of the leading AI labs, which have bet their architecture on building bigger LLMs and then count on faster hardware (and more of it) from Nvidia and other chipmakers to deliver improvements over time. If Inception is right about diffusion LLMs, then it would have big implications. The dilemma facing the AI industry is that improving model intelligence requires additional compute, and lots of it. Upgrading reasoning and increasing the number of agentic steps can typically increase costs and response time. So Inception's breakthrough on diffusion LLMs is all about faster AI response times and more efficient use of expensive GPU hardware, for now. The question remains whether it will be a niche use-case for more real-time AI applications or a bigger long-term challenger to the cutting edge frontier models.

news.author: Bloomberg
news.original_content:
Bloomberg:
Korean data-center company Elice falls 30%+ in Kosdaq trading debut; sources: Australian data center operator AirTrunk delays real estate investment trust IPO  —  Data-center infrastructure company Elice Inc. plunged in its trading debut in South Korea,
news.content_snippet: Data-center infrastructure company Elice Inc. plunged in its trading debut in South Korea, dragged down by swirling concern about the outlook for the industry.
news.summary_en: South Korean data center infrastructure firm Elice plunged more than 30% in its Kosdaq trading debut, while Australian operator AirTrunk postponed its real estate investment trust IPO. Secondary market investors are becoming increasingly skeptical of sky-high data center valuations, triggering a swift repricing of capital-intensive computing infrastructure.
news.title_zh: 亚太算力资产退潮：韩国数据中心首日破发三成
news.summary_zh: 韩国数据中心基础设施企业Elice上市首日暴跌超30%，澳大利亚数据中心巨头亦推迟信托上市

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 韩国数据中心基础设施运营商Elice在首尔科斯达克市场敲钟首日惨遭破发，股价盘中暴跌逾30%；与此同时，澳大利亚大型数据中心运营商AirTrunk也紧急搁置了其房地产投资信托的首次公开募股计划。二级市场对数据中心动辄百倍估值的故事开始失去耐心，高昂的电力折旧与巨额资本开支正在让盲目跟风的算力基建溢价迅速降温。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: South Korean data center infrastructure firm Elice plunged more than 30% in its Kosdaq trading debut, while Australian operator AirTrunk postponed its real estate investment trust IPO. news.original_content:
Reuters:
Sources: OpenAI is racing to secure investor commitments before Anthropic's expected IPO in mid-Nov. and aims to raise ~$30B; the round could value it at $1.4T+  —  OpenAI is racing to secure investor commitments before rival Anthropic's expected public m
news.content_snippet: OpenAI is racing to secure investor commitments before rival Anthropic's expected public market debut in mid-November …
news.summary_en: OpenAI is aggressively locking down investor commitments to close a massive $30 billion funding round at an eye-popping valuation north of $1.4 trillion, aiming to beat Anthropic's expected mid-November IPO. The preemptive strike is engineered to soak up sovereign and institutional liquidity before its fiercest rival taps public markets. With foundation model training costs spiraling out of control, the AI arms race has turned into an existential liquidity grab.

Sources: Ted Sarandos complained for months of a lack of new hit shows at Netflix and US watch time being down; it just fired its film chief and content chief  —  Company is overhauling creative leadership as it struggles to get domestic audie
news.content_snippet: Company is overhauling creative leadership as it struggles to get domestic audiences to watch more — Netflix is writing a new script.
news.summary_en: Netflix is overhauling its creative leadership after co-CEO Ted Sarandos voiced deep frustration over a prolonged lack of breakout hit shows and declining domestic watch time, resulting in the abrupt firing of its film and content chiefs. Confronted with the relentless drain of user attention toward short-form video and subscription saturation, the streaming titan is aggressively shedding mediocre, big-budget productions to defend its North American fortress.

news.title: Sources: Waymo aims to expand its fleet to 8K by the end of this year, up from 4K today, and to 20K by the end of 2027, after raising $5B in debt this month (Ellen DiMauro/Semafor)
news.title_en: Sources: Waymo aims to expand its fleet to 8K by the end of this year, up from 4K today, and to 20K by the end of 2027, after raising $5B in debt this month (Ellen DiMauro/Semafor)
news.author: Semafor
news.article_content:
As Waymo expands into new cities with its self-driving cars, the company plans to use the $5 billion it recently borrowed to massively increase its fleet.

The company, which currently has 4,000 cars, is looking to bring its total number to 8,000 by the end of the year and grow to 20,000 by the end of next year, according to people familiar with the matter.

Waymo declined to comment. The company said in a statement on its website that it raised the funds to grow internationally and in the US.

Waymo, which operates in 15 US cities, is also bringing its rides to locations such as Toronto. Waymo recently opened a facility in Nashville in partnership with Lyft to charge, clean and maintain cars.

Waymo has already ordered thousands of cars from China, to help expand its fleet, the New York Post reported. The company has also rebranded versions of a vehicle made by Zeekr, a unit of CCP-linked company Geely Holding Group.

Waymo recently raised debt for the first time, and it came without guarantees from Alphabet, its parent company. It borrowed the $5 billion from private credit lenders, and the deal allows the company to use its fleet in the future to borrow more by securitizing leases.

news.title_zh: 无母公司担保发债五十亿：文远知行竞争对手加速扩编
news.summary_zh: 自动驾驶领头羊Waymo在无母公司担保下举债50亿美元，计划三年内将车队扩充至两万辆
news.article_content_zh:
据了解，Waymo正计划利用本月最新筹集的50亿美元债务融资，将其自动驾驶车队规模从目前的4000辆在今年底翻倍至8000辆，并在2027年底前一举扩张至2万辆。这笔50亿美元的信贷融资具有划时代意义——它完全由私人信贷机构提供，母公司Alphabet未提供任何企业担保，且协议赋予Waymo未来通过车队租赁资产证券化继续发债融资的权利。

目前Waymo已在美国15个城市开通运营，并正在将足迹延展至多伦多等国际重镇。在地面基础设施端，Waymo近期在纳什维尔与Lyft合作建立了运营维护中心，负责车辆的日常充电、清洁与维保。与此同时，为了快速压低整车建造成本并保证供给，Waymo此前已从中国车企采购定制车辆，并换标使用吉利旗下极氪制造的专属Robotaxi底盘架构。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 自动驾驶领航者Waymo在无谷歌母公司担保的前提下，通过私募信贷机构成功举债50亿美元，并制定了激进的车队扩张路线图：计划在今年底将无人出租车规模由现存的4000辆翻倍至8000辆，并在2027年底冲刺至2万辆。随着业务跨入15座城市并拓展至多伦多，该公司正通过引入中国制造极氪车型降低造车成本，并探索车辆租赁资产证券化，彻底从实验室烧钱项目转型为自负盈亏的重资产商业闭环。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Waymo has raised $5 billion in debt from private credit lenders without parent guarantees from Alphabet, outlining a hyper-aggressive fleet expansion targeting 8,000 vehicles by year-end (up from 4,000) and 20,000 by 2027. Operating across 15 cities and expanding to international hubs like Toronto, the company is sourcing custom electric vehicles from Zeekr to drive down unit costs while planning fleet lease securitizations to cement a self-sustaining asset-heavy mobility business.

news.title: Cloudflare debuts Clairic, a System One-class extraction model it says processes unstructured data faster, more cheaply, and more accurately than normal LLMs (Cloudflare)
news.title_en: Cloudflare debuts Clairic, a System One-class extraction model it says processes unstructured data faster, more cheaply, and more accurately than normal LLMs (Cloudflare)
news.author: Cloudflare
news.article_content:
Today, we're announcing a preview of a new class of System One-style models: extraction models. Our first one, Clairic, is available hosted on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic.We intend to release the model open-weights soon. Clairic is an extraction model that is able to extract, compute, estimate, and forecast values from unstructured inputs — all at a significantly higher accuracy, faster latency, and cheaper cost than traditional LLMs.

When System One models were announced by TypeSafe a month ago, it took the industry by storm. As referenced by TypeSafe in their blog and defined by Daniel Kahneman’s book Thinking, Fast and Slow, a System One model should be fast and precise, which contrasts a System Two model that is capable of deliberate reasoning (like LLMs). With this, TypeSafe introduced Jev — a model that is purpose-fit for a specific use case, and priced accessibly given its niche domain. It excelled where LLMs failed, helping users make decisions based on probabilities and well-typed outputs. The introduction of Jev prompted people to start thinking about a new class of models that were not LLMs and how to integrate them into their workflows.

We were inspired by the concept of System One models and started thinking about other tasks where LLMs are inefficient. There are many structured-output calls going to frontier LLMs today with the same shapes again and again: What's the invoice total? When was this delivered? How many days late is it? What will this repair cost? What will traffic look like over the next 24 hours? None of these have answers you can list out in advance, which is needed for a decision model to give probabilities against. That led us to the class of models we're introducing today: System One extraction models.

Until now, every System One model has been a decision model: Jev and Clef take an input state and a list of questions and give probabilities against the inputs and your listed questions. Clairic is the first model in a new class: System One extraction models. It is still fast, typed, and cheap, but it answers with values directly extracted from the input, computed from it, or predicted beyond it.

Most model tasks ask for one of three kinds of output: a number, a choice from a fixed set, or open-ended text. Clairic handles the first, returning numbers with an 80% range, and also pulls typed values like names, dates and lists out of the input. Clef handles the second: it picks among options and returns a probability for each. LLMs handle the third. We call Clairic and Clef System One models because they answer in a single pass, without reasoning or generating tokens. They charge only for input and typically respond in under a second, while an LLM that reasons through the same step takes several seconds.

And because it generates no tokens, it can't produce a mistyped answer or “hallucinate” in the same way as an LLM (though it can, of course, make mistakes). Outputs are a value of the type you asked for, or null when the model fails to find an answer in the input. It also comes with confidence scores against the outputs to help you evaluate if it is appropriate to trust the model or to take a second look.

Here’s how extraction models fit into the landscape of System One and System Two models:

Typed values: spans, numbers, dates, times, lists, distributions, with calibrated probabilities

Which category is it? Is it legitimate? Which action should we take?

Why did it happen? How should we approach it? Can you fix it?

Yes: every answer is a value of its declared type (or null), inside your bounds

Together, these models can work together in unison to help you get closer to parsing through real-world data, making decisions on inputs, and then taking actions. Extraction models turn raw input into typed values, decision models turn values into decisions, and LLMs turn decisions into words.

Clairic is designed differently than an LLM. Similar to a decision model, it only processes input tokens with a single forward pass, and thus has no charge for output tokens. It is much faster, cheaper, and more accurate than an LLM for certain use cases.

A request is a state (the text to read, plus up to four optional images) and a map of typed fields. You name each field, give it a type and optional plain-language instructions, and get back one typed answer per field, all from one parallel pass. There is no reasoning and no output tokens – everything computes in a single forward pass, which means it is both fast and cheap.

A distribution inside your [min, max], on your step grid, linear or log scale.

Every scalar answer comes with p_null (the probability that the value isn’t in the inputs) and confidence. Every estimate answer comes with a median and an 80% interval (p10 to p90), plus all 99 percentiles on request. There's no limit on the number of fields: if they don't fit beside the input in one pass, the server splits them into parallel passes that each see the whole input, then merges the answers.

Here are some examples to illustrate the model’s features. Of course, using these features in a workflow would require appropriate inputs.

Extraction is probably the most common job handed to LLMs today: "return the invoice number, vendor and due date as JSON." It works most of the time, but the failure modes are hard to catch. The output may not be valid JSON, a digit can be misread as it's generated, and once a text excerpt comes back, there's no way to trace it to where it appeared in the source. Most people build extraction pipelines to combat this, with multiple layers of parsing, schema validation, retries and spot checks. On top of that, you pay for reasoning and output tokens on every field of every document.

Clairic operates differently; it doesn’t generate text answers. Instead, you get:

Let’s walk through an example to illustrate the ways Clairic can extract values from unstructured data and make estimates. Take a customer support email:

Hi, order A-88412 arrived on Sept 28, 2026 with a cracked screen and a dented corner. I paid $649.00 plus $52.10 tax. It's now Oct 9, 2026 and I'd like this fixed or refunded. Thanks, Dana

From a Worker, you would make a request to Clairic to process this data:

const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", {
  state: email,
  fields: {
    order_id:            { type: "text", instructions: "Order number" },
    delivered_on:        { type: "date", instructions: "Delivery date" },
    amount_paid:         { type: "number", decimals: 2, unit: "USD", instructions: "Total paid including tax" },
    days_since_delivery: { type: "duration", unit: "days", integer: true,
                           instructions: "Days from delivery to the date the customer wrote" },
    damage:              { type: "list", items: "text", instructions: "Each kind of damage described" },
    tracking_number:     { type: "text" },
  },
});globalThis.process??={},globalThis.process.env??={},document.querySelectorAll(`[data-code-copy]`).forEach(e=>{let t=e.closest(`.emdash-code`)?.querySelector(`pre code`);if(!t)return;let n=e.dataset.copyLabel??``,r=e.dataset.copiedLabel??``,i=null;e.addEventListener(`click`,()=>{navigator.clipboard.writeText(t.textContent??``).then(()=>{e.setAttribute(`data-copied`,``),e.setAttribute(`aria-label`,r),i&&clearTimeout(i),i=setTimeout(()=>{e.removeAttribute(`data-copied`),e.setAttribute(`aria-label`,n),i=null},1500)}).catch(e=>{console.warn(`code-copy: clipboard write failed`,e)})})});Clairic returns the extracted values, spans in the input, probability that it is null (p_null) and confidence score:

  },
  "amount_paid": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 1.6e-5,
    "guess": 701.1,

  },
  "days_since_delivery": {
    "type": "duration",
    "p_null": 6.1e-9,
    "unit": "days",
    "guess": 11,
    "confidence": 0.999999,
    "value": 11
  },
  "damage": {
    "type": "list",
    "value": ["cracked screen", "dented corner"],
    "spans": [[50, 64], [71, 84]]
  },
  "tracking_number": {
    "type": "text",
    "p_null": 1,

Here’s a real-life photo of a receipt — the text is not perfect and the angle of the image doesn’t help its legibility. We passed this image to Clairic to see what it could extract:

   },

    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 5.2313655629632194e-08,
    "guess": 2,
    "confidence": 0.9997007500403496,
    "value": 2
   },
   "unit_price": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 0.001599092734977603,
    "guess": 7.99,
    "confidence": 0.9991279019989127,
    "value": 7.99
   },
   "subtotal": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 9.69956488461321e-08,
    "guess": 15.98,
    "confidence": 0.9999881983893096,
    "value": 15.98
   },
   "sales_tax": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 2.5511653802823275e-06,
    "guess": 0,
    "confidence": 0.9999800924450729,
    "value": 0
   },
   "tip": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 5.953857908025384e-05,
    "guess": 2.39,
    "confidence": 0.9335768781214697,

}As you can see, it was able to extract all the values from the images, alongside a confidence score. It also correctly stated that there was no discount shown in the receipt, giving the value as null.

Some values aren't in the input at all, but the input carries evidence for them. For example, values might not be in plain text but can be discerned from values around it. If you ask an LLM for an estimation, you usually get a single number with no sense of how sure the model is. It will make safe guesses or hallucinate, or reason its way around the answer. If you land on an estimate, any downstream processing can't tell a confident $180 from an unconfident $180, so it can't help you decide what is appropriate to automate in the circumstances. It is also a lot slower and more expensive to do reasoning through LLMs.

A decision model can approximate an estimate by choosing among buckets ("under $100", "$100–500", …), but buckets are coarse, every bucket adds input tokens, and each new category adds more sources of confusion for the model during its decision making process.

Clairic returns a distribution over the range you declare: a point value, a median, an 80% interval, and every percentile on request. The estimate is designed to fall inside your bounds, so there's nothing to clamp or round afterward. The width of the interval reflects data confidence: a narrow range signals high certainty, while a wide range indicates low certainty, information you can use to route another check.

The width of the interval reflects data confidence: a narrow range signals high certainty, while a wide range indicates low certainty, information you can use to route another check.

Leah Nylen / Bloomberg:

The settlement mandates that Publicis guarantee equal, non-discriminatory access to LiveRamp's essential data tools for all competing agencies and advertisers.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 美国联邦贸易委员会通过了一项附带限制条款的和解令，正式批准全球广告巨头阳狮集团以22亿美元收购数据连接服务商LiveRamp的交易。作为反垄断放行的核心交换条件，协议强制要求合并后的实体必须为所有客户及竞品广告商提供平等、无歧视的LiveRamp核心数据连接工具访问权限。监管机构此举意在防止跨国代理集团借机垄断数字营销生态链的关键身份识别与隐私数据管道。

elements_en.who: CoreWeave and Wall Street private credit debt markets
elements_en.where: US high-yield bond and equities markets
elements_en.what: Bond yields touched distressed debt thresholds, cratering equity value by over 20%
elements_en.why: Heavy reliance on aggressive debt financing to buy depreciating GPUs sparks liquidity panic when end-user returns slow

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 用还没焐热的显卡做抵押，借天价高利贷去抢下一批显卡，这种左脚踩右脚上天的‘庞氏飞轮’终于卡壳了。当债券市场开始把AI算力当垃圾债折价甩卖时，说明华尔街的算盘打明白了：显卡会年年贬值，但银行的利息可一分都不会少。CoreWeave这一摔，不知道要惊醒多少还在做千亿云服务美梦的PPT吹鼓手。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Collateralizing today’s GPUs to take out high-yield debt to buy tomorrow’s GPUs was an ingenious flywheel right up until basic math caught up. When bonds slip into distressed territory, it means credit markets realized hardware depreciates fast while debt compounding never sleeps. This cold shower reminds everyone that AI datacenters aren't magical money printers.
ai_analysis.digest_zh: 头部AI算力云基础设施商CoreWeave发行的债券利差上周飙升超过1000个基点，按照金融市场通用定义已正式跌入困境债务区间。华尔街知名投资人相继发声警告AI算力建设背后暗藏的巨额私募信贷泡沫，导致CoreWeave股价周跌幅超过20%，并迅速波及整个AI概念股产业链。事件起因在于该公司此前凭借英伟达GPU做高杠杆抵押借款进行激进算力扩张，其现金流造血速度正面临严峻的市场拷问。
ai_analysis.digest_en: Bonds issued by AI cloud infrastructure unicorn CoreWeave plummeted into distressed territory as yield spreads widened over 1,000 basis points. Market fears surrounding private credit exposure to hyper-leveraged GPU deployments triggered a 20%+ share slump, triggering broader contagion concerns across the AI hardware sector.

news.content_snippet: This voice experience is generated by AI. Learn more. … Want to make your dumb robot smart? $3 an hour is all it costs.
news.summary_en: Robotics foundation model startup Dream Labs secured a massive $90 million seed round led by B Capital and Kindred Ventures. The company is developing Dream-1, a robotics foundation model trained directly on human demonstration videos, providing API access for diverse physical hardware platforms.
news.title_zh: 机器人基座初创公司完成九千万美元巨额种子轮

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 具身智能初创企业Dream Labs宣布完成规模达9000万美元的种子轮融资，由顶级风投机构联合领投。该团队推出了名为Dream-1的机器人通用基础模型，其技术路径核心在于纯粹通过吸收人类操作日常行为的视频数据进行预训练，并计划将这套多模态具身能力以云端API形式向第三方硬件厂商开放。本轮融资充分证明资本市场正从大语言模型转向抢跑具身物理AI控制大脑。

Training robots to manipulate reality just by watching YouTube sounds brilliant in pitch decks, but between video pixels and a jerky robotic claw crushing coffee cups, there lies a painful engineering chasm.

news.author: Bloomberg
news.original_content:
Paige Smith / Bloomberg:
Ramp says it applied to the US OCC for a trust bank charter that, if approved, would allow it to offer fiduciary investment management and digital asset custody  —  Financial technology firm Ramp said it applied with the Office of the Comp
news.content_snippet: Financial technology firm Ramp said it applied with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency for a trust bank charter …
news.summary_en: Fintech unicorn Ramp filed an application with the US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) for a national trust bank charter. If granted, the charter would empower Ramp to offer fiduciary investment management services and custody digital assets for its commercial clients.
news.title_zh: 金融科技巨头申办信托银行牌照，剑指数字资产托管
news.summary_zh: 支出管理独角兽Ramp向美监管申请信托银行牌照，获批后将可提供受托投资与数字资产托管

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 知名企业财务与支出自动化管理平台Ramp已向美国货币监理署（OCC）正式递交全国性信托银行牌照申请。如果顺利获批，该牌照将赋予Ramp直接提供受托投资管理以及数字资产合规托管等高阶金融服务的能力。Ramp此举旨在从单一的账单与报销Saas工具升级为受联邦严格监管的金融全周期账户，以锁定企业客户的闲置现金管理与加密资产业务。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Fintech unicorn Ramp filed an application with the US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) for a national trust bank charter. If granted, the charter would empower Ramp to offer fiduciary investment management services and custody digital assets for its commercial clients.

elements_zh.who: 金融科技独角兽Ramp及美国货币监理署（OCC）

elements_zh.what: 申请全国信托银行牌照，以获权从事信托资管与数字资产托管业务

elements_en.who: Fintech unicorn Ramp and US OCC regulators
elements_en.what: Applied for a national trust bank charter covering fiduciary services and crypto custody
elements_en.why: Eliminating intermediary banking friction to capture corporate treasury yields and enterprise digital asset management

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 所有发企业信用卡的软件公司，终极梦想都是把手伸进客户的钱包底盘当银行家。给企业管发票只能赚点过路费，要是能把客户的闲钱乃至比特币名正言顺地锁在自己的托管池里，那才叫旱涝保收。披着极简软件外皮的SaaS新贵，最后活成了它当年扬言要颠覆的华尔街老银行。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Every corporate expense management SaaS eventually realizes that parsing receipts is chump change compared to actually being a bank. If you can legally sit on enterprise treasuries and custody their crypto, you've hit peak fintech. They spent years mocking traditional banks, only to realize the endgame is literally becoming one.

news.title: Sources: Nscale is in talks for a second deal with Anthropic worth ~$45B to deliver 460MW of computing power at its West Virginia campus using Vera Rubin chips (Bloomberg)

news.author: Bloomberg
news.original_content:
Bloomberg:
Sources: Nscale is in talks for a second deal with Anthropic worth ~$45B to deliver 460MW of computing power at its West Virginia campus using Vera Rubin chips  —  Nscale Ltd., the AI cloud computing firm, is in talks to sell computing power to Anthropi
news.content_snippet: Nscale Ltd., the AI cloud computing firm, is in talks to sell computing power to Anthropic PBC in a deal that could be worth about $45 billion …
news.summary_en: Emerging AI cloud firm Nscale is negotiating a landmark computing power contract with Anthropic valued at approximately $45 billion. The proposed agreement calls for Nscale to provide 460 megawatts of high-density capacity utilizing next-generation Vera Rubin chips from its West Virginia datacenter campus.
news.title_zh: 算力服务商或获四百五十亿美元大单，向大模型厂供电
news.summary_zh: 算力基础设施商Nscale正与Anthropic洽谈450亿美元大单，提供460兆瓦下一代算力

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 新兴AI云算力服务商Nscale目前正与大模型独角兽Anthropic深入洽谈一笔价值高达约450亿美元的算力采购补充协议。按照拟议条款，Nscale将在其位于西弗吉尼亚州的数据中心园区，基于下一代先进芯片架构向Anthropic稳定交付高达460兆瓦（MW）的超高密度计算基础设施。这一天文数字级的交易凸显了顶级模型厂商在训练下一代前沿多模态大模型时对长周期算力与能源的饥渴争夺。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Emerging AI cloud firm Nscale is negotiating a landmark computing power contract with Anthropic valued at approximately $45 billion. The proposed agreement calls for Nscale to provide 460 megawatts of high-density capacity utilizing next-generation Vera Rubin chips from its West Virginia datacenter campus.

elements_zh.why: 大模型厂商必须提前数年抢占超万卡集群所需的电力接入与未来一代硬件产能

elements_en.who: AI cloud infrastructure provider Nscale and Anthropic
elements_en.what: In talks for a ~$45B contract to deliver 460MW of computing infrastructure with Vera Rubin chips
elements_en.why: Hyperscalers need to lock down massive power reserves and future-gen silicon allocations years ahead

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 张嘴就是450亿美金加460兆瓦电力，这胃口哪是在训练算法，分明是在修赛博三峡大坝。连芯片都直接锁定到未来的鲁宾架构，说明顶级玩家已经彻底接受了现实：搞AGI不是比谁代码写得漂亮，就是纯粹的‘烧钱堆电量’。只要VC和云厂商敢掏钱，这帮AI巨头就能把整个州的电网全部买空。
ai_analysis.insight_en: A casual $45 billion for 460 megawatts—Anthropic isn't training algorithms; they're attempting to power a small sovereign nation with pure silicon. Locking down unreleased Rubin chips years in advance proves AGI development is less about poetic software and more about who can scorch through an entire state's electrical grid the fastest.
